The passage sits among ayat about religious authority and about wealth held by those who teach.

keyTerms.note: The Quran names the mouth when it marks speech unsupported by anything behind it. The phrase occurs three times in this surah, twice within three ayat, each time weighing a claim rather than answering one.
A verb meaning to make one thing look like another. The charge is of repeating a formula inherited from older communities rather than of arriving at it, which is why no counter-argument is offered.
From a root meaning to overturn or divert. The passive leaves the agent unnamed, so the closing question asks how a view takes hold rather than who is to be blamed for it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina in that decade held Jewish and Christian neighbours, traders and travelling monks from the north, and Arabs who had heard scriptural stories at fairs without ever reading anything. Doctrine circulated as recited formula rather than as text, passed between camps and market stalls. A person could hold a phrase for a lifetime having never met the community that produced it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a claim made out of the mouth occurs six times in the Quran, three of them in this surah and two within three ayat of each other. It is used at 9:8 of a treaty offered insincerely and at 9:32 of an attempt to put out a light, so one image is applied here to three different subjects.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a doctrinal claim as an object with a history rather than as a proposition to be refuted. That is a particular move: it asks where a saying came from rather than whether it can be defended. The closing question about being turned away then locates the difficulty in a process, which keeps the ayah from resolving into a verdict on the people holding it.

crossReferences.why: Responds to the same kind of claim at length, describing the enormity of attributing a son to God.
Denies begetting and being begotten in the shortest statement the Quran makes anywhere.
Records a different claim of special closeness to God and answers it by pointing to accountability.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you believe firmly and trace where you first heard it. Not whether it is true. Just where it came from, from whom, and whether you have examined it since. The method used here is historical rather than argumentative, and applying it to yourself is far more uncomfortable than applying it to anyone else.

studies.title: Lords Beside God
studies.meaning: The charge is not that anyone was called a god. It is that obedience was given where it should not have been, and the passage names that as taking lords beside God. The classical explanation is specific: religious authorities were followed in declaring things permitted and forbidden, and that following is what the word describes. The ayah then states what had actually been asked of them, which was to worship one God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing directly from the previous ayah. The commentaries preserve a well-known exchange in which a listener objected that his people had never worshipped their scholars, and was answered that obedience in matters of what is permitted and forbidden was exactly what the word meant. That explanation is the standard one across the classical commentaries on this ayah.

keyTerms.note: A term for the religious scholars of earlier communities, used in the Quran for teaching authority rather than for ritual office. It names the people who settled questions, which is what this ayah is about.
The plural of a word for an owner or master who is obeyed. Arabic applied it to ordinary authority as well as to God, so the charge concerns the kind of obedience rather than a title.
From a root meaning to move freely, used of God being far removed from what is attributed to Him. The formula works as a denial expressed in praise rather than as an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religious learning was scarce and personal. A community might have one or two men who could read a scripture, and their judgement settled disputes about what was allowed at a wedding, a funeral or a market stall. Nobody could check them, because nobody else could read the text. The authority described here was real, useful, and almost impossible to question from below.
studies.didYouKnow: The commentaries on this ayah preserve an exchange in which someone objected that his people had never worshipped their scholars, and was told that obeying them when they made forbidden things permitted was precisely what the ayah described. That explanation, rather than any argument about titles, is what the classical tradition transmits alongside the passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage relocates the danger. It lies not in what anyone is called but in where a decision is finally made, which means a person can hold entirely correct beliefs and still be described here. That keeps religious authority a live question rather than a settled one, and it does so without denying that scholars are needed, since the objection is to substitution rather than to consultation.

crossReferences.why: Calls to common ground: that none among us take others as lords beside God.
Continues immediately with the wealth held by the same class of religious authority.
Asks about partners who lay down in religion what God has not permitted.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you do because someone you respect said so, and that you have never checked yourself. Not to reject it. Just to find the reason, if there is one, and to sit with the gap if there is not. This ayah is about where a decision actually gets made, and most of us have never looked.

studies.title: Blowing At A Light
studies.meaning: The image is domestic and slightly absurd: people trying to blow out a light with their mouths. It is the same phrase used two ayat earlier of a claim made without grounding, turned now toward an attempt to stop something. The reply is not that they will fail but that God refuses anything except completing that light. The second ayah restates it as a purpose, and both close on the same concession about dislike.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the passage on doctrinal claims and preceding the long section on the march north. The commentators read the two ayat as one statement, the first denying that the light can be put out and the second naming who sent it and to what end. The second appears in nearly identical wording at 48:28 and again at 61:9, both Medinan.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for putting out a lamp or a cooking fire. It carries no grandeur at all, which is the point: an enormous intention described with the vocabulary of a small domestic act.

A strong verb of refusal, used of someone declining outright rather than of preventing. The sentence sets God's refusal against their wanting, so two wills face each other rather than a power facing a plan.
From a root for appearing and also for the back or upper side. Commentators differ over whether it means becoming manifest, becoming uppermost, or both, and they record the readings together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A lamp was a wick in a clay dish of oil, and it went out constantly: a draught through a doorway, a moth, someone walking past too quickly. Every household knew the reflex of shielding one with a cupped hand while crossing a room. The image would have arrived as ordinary rather than poetic, and its comedy is that the thing being blown at is not that kind of light.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat occurs three times in the Quran in almost identical words: here, at 48:28 and at 61:9, each time closing on a clause about somebody disliking it. Surah 61 also carries the image of extinguishing God's light with the mouth, so the whole pairing recurs there as a unit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers opposition by describing the opponent's action rather than their argument, and the description is deliberately undignified. That is a claim about scale: the effort and its object are not in the same order of magnitude. It also grounds the outcome in God's refusal rather than in the community's strength, which removes any suggestion that the light depends on who is defending it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of extinguishing God's light with the mouth, in another Medinan surah.
Repeats the second of these ayat almost word for word, with a different closing clause.
Develops the image of light at length, as a lamp inside glass inside a niche.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are spending effort on something whose outcome does not actually depend on you. Not in order to stop caring. Just to name it once, honestly, and see what that does to the anxiety attached to it. The ayah is not telling anyone to sit still; it is setting the size of an effort beside the size of its object.

studies.title: Gold Put In The Ground
studies.meaning: Two charges sit side by side and the second is wider than the first. Many among the religious learned of earlier communities consume people's wealth wrongfully and bar the way to God. Then the sentence opens out and names nobody in particular: those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it. No office is attached to the second clause, which is how the passage reaches whoever is listening.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the ayah about obedience given to religious authority. The commentators note the shift mid-sentence from a specific class of people to an unrestricted description. They differ over what hoarding means here: some read it as wealth on which the due share was never paid, others as accumulation held back from any spending at all, and both readings are recorded.

keyTerms.note: The Quran uses eating for taking wealth wrongly, which makes the act bodily and appetitive rather than financial. The construction here is emphatic, adding a note of insistence to the charge being laid.
The word means empty, false, without foundation. Applied to a transaction it names one lacking any real basis rather than one that is merely unfair, so it covers payment given for nothing.
From the word for buried treasure. The verb occurs only here in the Quran and pictures wealth put away out of circulation rather than wealth simply possessed, which is what the commentators discuss.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Coin in that economy was scarce and physical. Gold and silver arrived through trade with the north and the south, and a family's savings might be a bag under a floor or coins sewn into a belt. Money that went into the ground stopped working: it fed nobody, financed no caravan, employed no one. Hoarding was visible in its effects long before anybody counted anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for hoarding occurs only once in the Quran, here, and the noun from the same root is the word used for the buried treasure belonging to two orphaned boys at 18:82. The image is therefore of wealth put underground, which is why the punishment described in the very next ayah is made of the same metal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a charge against religious authority and a charge against ordinary accumulation in one sentence with nothing between them. That denies the listener the comfort of hearing the ayah as being about somebody else. And by describing the fault as wealth taken out of circulation rather than wealth possessed, it locates the problem in what money is not doing rather than in how much of it there is.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately with what becomes of the hoarded metal on the day of judgement.
Describes a man counting his wealth and supposing that it will make him last forever.
Warns those who are stingy with what God gave them, describing what it becomes for them.

studies.applyIt: Look at the money you are holding that has no purpose attached to it, only a feeling. Give a small part of it away this week to something specific enough to name out loud. The ayah is not against saving. It is about wealth that has stopped moving, and the remedy it implies is movement rather than emptiness.

studies.title: This Is What You Stored
studies.meaning: The image is exact and physical. The metal itself is heated and then applied to three places on the body: the forehead, the sides, the back. A sentence is spoken over it, this is what you stored for yourselves, and the person is told to taste what they were storing. Nothing is substituted for the wealth. The same object returns, in a different state, and speaks for itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing directly from the previous ayah. The commentators discuss the choice of the three places branded, several connecting them to the way a man avoids someone asking him for help: turning the face away, then the shoulder, then the back. The passage belongs to a section of the surah concerned with wealth held back while contributions were being asked for.

keyTerms.note: The verb for cauterising with hot metal, which was an ordinary medical treatment of the period. The vocabulary comes from healing rather than from punishment, and that is part of the image's force.
The first of three places named. Commentators frequently link the three to the successive turnings of a body away from someone who is asking, so the list traces a refusal rather than naming surfaces.
The Quran uses tasting for meeting a consequence directly rather than being told about it. The verb makes the encounter first-hand, which is exactly the difference the passage is drawing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cauterising was real medicine. A wound that would not close, a bite, a swelling: the treatment was a heated iron, and everyone had either seen it done or had it done to them. Branding also marked ownership on camels, burnt into the hide in a pattern that identified the owner across a whole region. Both associations sit under this image.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for hoarding appears twice inside this single ayah, once as a verb and once as a noun, having already appeared in the ayah before it. The repetition puts the same term in the act of the one storing and in the sentence spoken over him, so the consequence is described using the vocabulary of the deed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not replace the wealth with something else. The same metal returns, which makes the outcome a disclosure rather than an exchange. That is a claim about how consequence works here: what a person accumulated is what meets them, in a form that shows what it was. And the sentence is spoken in the second person, addressed to the individual rather than said about him.

crossReferences.why: States the charge whose outcome this ayah describes, in the same continuous sentence.
Says what is hoarded will be hung about the neck on the day of resurrection.
Describes a fire that reaches the hearts, in a surah about counting up wealth.

studies.applyIt: Notice the second half of the sentence spoken here: what you stored for yourselves. Take one thing you are holding back and ask who exactly it is being kept for. If the honest answer is a version of yourself who may never arrive, that is worth knowing before anything gets decided about it.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Twelve Months In The Decree
studies.meaning: A number is stated and then grounded: twelve months, written in God's decree from the day the heavens and the earth were made, of which four are sacred. The grounding is the argument, because the passage concerns a count that had been tampered with. An instruction follows not to wrong yourselves during them, and then a clause about fighting collectively as they fight collectively. A calendar is being restored, not invented.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, part of the proclamation section. The commentators connect this ayah and the next to a practice of shifting which month counted as sacred so that raiding could continue without any truce appearing to be broken. The four months named in the tradition are three that run together and one standing apart, and the passage states the reckoning as fixed.

keyTerms.note: The word means a count or a reckoned period and is used elsewhere for waiting times. Naming the number rather than the months puts the weight on arithmetic that had been altered by someone.
The second word means straight or self-maintaining. Commentators read the phrase of an order that holds itself steady, and note that religion here covers the reckoning of time as much as belief.
An adverb meaning entirely or as one body. It appears twice in the same clause, applied to both sides equally, so the sentence describes a symmetry rather than granting a general licence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months were working infrastructure. Trade fairs, pilgrimage and the settling of debts all happened under their protection, because a caravan could move without an escort and a man could enter a rival's territory safely. Everyone's year was organised around them. Altering which month counted meant a merchant setting out could no longer know whether he was safe on the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming twelve occurs only once in the whole Quran, here, and the ayah dates the count to the creation of the heavens and the earth rather than to any human arrangement. That grounding is unusual: a dispute about a calendar is settled by placing the number beyond the reach of the people arguing over it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats time as given rather than agreed, and the consequence follows. If the count was fixed at creation, then a community adjusting it for convenience is not managing its own affairs but altering something it does not own. And the instruction is phrased as not wronging yourselves, which turns an interference with a shared calendar into an injury done by the interferer to himself.

crossReferences.why: Describes the practice of postponement directly, which this ayah's fixed count is answering.
Explains the crescent moons as measures of time for people and for the pilgrimage.
States that sun and moon were measured out so that the years could be reckoned.

studies.applyIt: Look at a boundary in your week that you keep moving because moving it is convenient: a stopping time, a day off, an hour that was meant for one thing. Put it back this week and leave it alone once. Notice what the adjusting had quietly been protecting you from having to face.

studies.title: Keeping The Count, Losing The Point
studies.meaning: A practice is named and then taken apart. Postponement is called an increase in disbelief, and the mechanism is spelled out: a month permitted one year and forbidden the next, in order to keep the total God made sacred while allowing what He had disallowed. The arithmetic is preserved and the substance is emptied. What is described is a procedure for keeping a rule's appearance and removing its effect.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the ayah that fixes the count of months. The commentators describe the practice as an announcement made at the pilgrimage by those holding the authority to declare it, shifting which month would be treated as sacred that year so that fighting could go on. Reports differ over the details of how it was managed, and the commentaries record the variation.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to delay or put off. It occurs only here in the Quran, so the commentaries reconstruct the practice it names from historical reports rather than from any parallel passage.

keyTerms.gloss: so as to make it match
keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to make one thing tread in step with another. It describes an arithmetic being brought into agreement while the substance underneath is quietly changed.
A passive with the agent unnamed, used repeatedly in the Quran of wrongdoing that has come to look reasonable from inside. The construction leaves the process undescribed and its effect exact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The authority to declare a month's status was itself an office, held by a particular family and announced publicly during the pilgrimage. The declaration bound the tribes present, and a man's plans for a whole year turned on it. Because everyone accepted the count, the count could be used: nobody was openly breaking a rule, and everyone knew the season had moved anyway.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for this practice occurs only once in the entire Quran. The classical commentators therefore reconstruct what it was from historical reports rather than from other passages, and their accounts of the mechanics differ in detail while agreeing entirely about the effect it produced.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a specific moral technique: keeping the form of an obligation while removing what the form was for. Calling that an increase rather than a violation is precise, since nothing was openly broken. And by adding that the wrongdoing had been made to look good to those doing it, the ayah accounts for how such a procedure survives without anyone involved feeling dishonest.

crossReferences.why: Fixes the count that this practice preserved in appearance while emptying it in substance.
Addresses a different piece of ritual reasoning that kept a form while losing its point.
Describes prayer performed to be seen, the same substitution of appearance for substance.

studies.applyIt: Find a rule you keep to the letter in a way that removes its point: a deadline met with something unfinished, a promise kept in words only. Name one this week and either do the thing properly or drop the pretence. This failure gets named so precisely because it never feels like one from the inside.

studies.title: You Grew Heavy Toward The Ground
studies.meaning: The question is asked with something close to exasperation, and its central word is physical. Told to move out, you made yourselves heavy toward the earth. Then the question widens: have you settled for this life instead of what follows. The answer given is a measurement rather than a rebuke. The provision of this life, set against the next, is only a little. Nothing is said about it being bad.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, opening the surah's long section on the expedition north toward Tabuk. The march fell in intense summer heat, at harvest time, across a long distance, toward a frontier held by an organised power. The commentators describe reluctance that was genuine and widespread, and the surah argues with it at length rather than dismissing it in a line.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of an animal startling and bolting, and of a group setting out quickly. It carries speed and reluctance overcome, which is why the answering image in the same sentence is weight.
A reflexive form meaning to make oneself heavy. It occurs only here in the Quran and pictures a body settling toward the ground rather than a decision being taken by anyone.
The word for goods a traveller carries and uses up along the road. It names something genuinely useful whose defining feature is that it gets consumed and left behind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The march north fell at the worst possible time. Dates were ripening, wells along the route lay far apart, and the heat made daytime travel dangerous. Men with orchards stood to lose a whole year's crop by leaving. The reluctance the ayah describes was not cowardice in the ordinary sense; it was the arithmetic of a farmer looking at fruit that would not wait.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for making oneself heavy occurs only once in the Quran, here, and it is built on the ordinary word for weight. The image is not of refusal but of gravity, a body sinking toward the ground, which is why the answer that follows weighs two things against each other rather than talking about courage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not call the present life worthless. It calls it little, which is a comparison rather than a dismissal, and the difference matters for how a reader treats ordinary attachments. The question asked is about contentment: whether a person has settled. That puts the fault in a stopping point rather than in whatever was being enjoyed along the way.

crossReferences.why: States that the life of this world, next to the hereafter, is only a passing enjoyment.
Says plainly that people prefer this life while the next is better and lasting.
Gives the answering instruction: move out light or heavy, in whatever condition you are.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have gone heavy this week: something you agreed to and then found reasons not to begin. Do the first ten minutes of it today, before the reasons finish assembling themselves. The ayah describes a body settling rather than a mind refusing, and bodies are moved by starting rather than by deciding.

studies.title: You Will Not Harm Him
studies.meaning: Three consequences are named and the third is the one that lands. If you do not go out, a painful punishment; He will replace you with another people; and you will not harm Him at all. The second clause says the work does not require these particular hands. The last removes the remaining assumption, that a refusal is at least a blow struck somewhere. It is not, and that is where the sentence stops.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the question about growing heavy. The commentators read the three clauses as escalating, and they note that the threat of substitution appears elsewhere in the Quran addressed to different audiences. This section belongs to the run-up to the march north, when participation and contributions were being asked for and some were withheld.

keyTerms.note: A verb of exchange, used of substituting one thing for another of the same kind. It treats a community as replaceable in a role, which is the specific discomfort this clause produces.
Deliberately unspecified. The commentators decline to identify who is meant, noting that the phrase draws its force from vagueness rather than from any prediction it might be making.

keyTerms.gloss: and you will not harm Him
keyTerms.note: The verb for causing injury or loss. Placed last, it removes the only consolation available to anyone withholding cooperation, which is the belief that the withholding registers somewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a tribal setting, withdrawal was leverage. A clan declining to join an expedition weakened it measurably, and everyone counted who arrived. Refusal was a recognised way of registering a complaint and it usually produced a negotiation. This ayah addresses people for whom that arithmetic was second nature, and it removes the arithmetic rather than arguing with the complaint.
studies.didYouKnow: The threat of replacement by another people appears several times in the Quran, at 47:38 and 4:133 among others, always addressed to a community rather than to individuals and never naming who the replacement would be. Classical commentary on this ayah routinely gathers those passages together and reads them as one warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies that God has needs, at exactly the point where a community might have begun to feel indispensable. That has two effects at once. It removes the leverage of withholding, and it removes the pride of taking part, since being used is not the same as being required. What remains is that the invitation was worth accepting for the sake of the one accepting it.

crossReferences.why: Warns a community that turning away brings a replacement who will not be like them.
States that people are the ones in need of God, who is free of all need.
Describes a people God would bring in place of those who turn back from their faith.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you contribute where you have quietly assumed you could not be replaced: at work, in a family, in a group you belong to. Consider for one honest minute that it would carry on without you. The point is not to feel small. It is to see how much of your reason for turning up rested on being needed.

studies.title: Second Of Two In The Cave
studies.meaning: The sentence opens with a conditional that is almost a shrug: if you do not help him, he has been helped already. What follows is a memory offered as evidence, told in a chain of clauses each beginning with when, which holds the scene in the present. The reassurance quoted is a single short sentence. Then four things God is said to have done, none of them visible at the time to the two men inside the rock.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage urging a community reluctant to set out on a hard expedition. The memory recalled is the migration from Mecca, when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and one companion hid in a cave while search parties looked for them. The commentators treat the reference as well known to its audience, which is why no narrative detail is given beyond what the argument needs.

keyTerms.note: A hollow in rock rather than a cavern, the kind of shelter a traveller uses. The definite article assumes the hearer knows which one, so the ayah is recalling a story rather than telling it.
From a root for settling and stillness, related to the word for a dwelling. It names a calm that descends and settles rather than one a person achieves, which is why the verb used is sending down.
A superlative in the feminine, matching the word for an utterance. Two claims are set on a vertical scale, and the outcome is described as a position occupied rather than as an argument won.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pursuit in the desert was a tracking skill. Bedouin trackers could read a person's weight, pace and direction from disturbed sand, and Mecca offered a substantial bounty for the two men. Hiding in country you did not control meant sitting still while people who knew the ground searched it. The cave lay south of the city, against the expected direction of flight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for tranquillity appears six times in the Quran and never of something a person produces. Five describe it being sent down, onto the Prophet here, onto believers at a moment of fear, into their hearts before a pledge. The sixth places it inside the ark carried by the Children of Israel. The term is shared with related languages of the region, where a similar word names the divine presence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Help is presented as something that has already happened, which changes what the reluctant listener is being asked for. Their assistance is not needed for the outcome; it is offered to them as an opportunity. The ayah also locates support in things nobody saw, a calm and unseen forces, so the evidence for divine help is survival rather than spectacle. The two men are named only as a companion and a second.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for tranquillity sent down, after a moment when numbers had failed.
Describes the same descent of calm into believers' hearts, increasing their faith.
Shows a similar instruction not to grieve, given to the mother of Moses.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment you got through that you had been certain you would not. You did not arrange the part that saved you. This ayah argues backwards from exactly that kind of memory, and keeping one specific instance in mind is more use in a crisis than any general statement about trust.

studies.title: Light Or Heavy, Go Out
studies.meaning: The instruction is two words wide and it covers everyone. Go out light or heavy. The pair is deliberately open, and the commentators fill it with several readings: young and old, mounted and on foot, rich and poor, willing and reluctant. None is chosen over the others. The striving is then specified as being with property and person, and the whole thing closes on a conditional about knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, at the point of departure for the march north. The commentators report that people arrived in every condition, some fully equipped and others with nothing at all, and that the phrase was understood at the time to close off every available excuse. The ayat immediately before and after it address those who found a reason not to come.

keyTerms.note: A pair occurring only once in the Quran. The commentators offer several readings, young and old, mounted and on foot, willing and reluctant, and set them side by side without choosing between them.
From a root meaning effort carried to the point of hardship. The word covers exertion of every kind and takes its content in this ayah from the phrase that follows it.
A conditional close that suspends the whole statement on the listener's own understanding rather than asserting it over them. The Quran uses it where a claim cannot be demonstrated in advance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Equipping a man for a long march was expensive. He needed a mount or a share in one, water skins, provisions and a weapon, and many households simply could not manage it. Some came asking to be carried and had to be turned away because nothing could be found. The word light would have applied to those men quite literally.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words rendered light and heavy occurs only once in the Quran, and the classical commentators list many different readings of it side by side without ever choosing between them. The breadth is treated as deliberate: a phrase kept open so that no condition could be produced afterwards as an exemption.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage declines to define its own terms, and the declining does the work. By naming a pair of opposites rather than a category, it covers the whole range between them and leaves nobody outside it. That is how a general call is issued without producing a list, and it returns the question of whether someone qualifies to that person rather than to anyone else.

crossReferences.why: Names the conditions that genuinely do excuse a person, later in the same section.
Distinguishes those who strive with property and person from those who remain behind.
Poses the reluctance this instruction answers, describing it as growing heavy.

studies.applyIt: Take the condition you usually cite for not starting something: tired, busy, not ready, not qualified. Then do a small version of the thing anyway, today, in exactly that condition. This phrase was framed so that no state of readiness could count as a precondition, which is worth testing once on something ordinary.

studies.title: The Distance Was Too Far
studies.meaning: The analysis begins with a hypothetical and is unsparing. Had there been a near gain and an easy journey, they would have come. The distance is what decided it. Then the passage moves to what they will say afterwards, swearing by God that they would have marched if they had been able. The verdict is not that they were cowardly. It is that the oath is false, and that it is ruining them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, during or after the march north. The commentators place these ayat among those addressing people in Medina who stayed behind and offered reasons afterwards. The distance to the frontier was unusually long by the standards of earlier expeditions. The surah returns repeatedly to the excuses given, treating the swearing rather than the staying as the matter at hand.

keyTerms.note: The first word means something incidental that presents itself, used throughout the Quran of worldly gain. Pairing it with near names the exact attraction: not wealth as such, but wealth soon.
From a root meaning to split or to be arduous. It occurs only here in the Quran and names a journey by what it costs rather than by how far it runs, which is what the sentence measures.
The verb for ruin and perishing, taking the self as its object. The damage runs inward, so a false oath is treated as an injury to the one swearing rather than a deception of anybody else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An expedition's appeal was normally calculated in the open. Men weighed distance, season, likely return and risk, and nobody pretended otherwise. What this passage isolates is the second step: having made that calculation, presenting the result afterwards as an incapacity. In a society where a man's oath was his standing, swearing to a reason you knew was not the reason cost more than staying home.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the hard journey occurs only once in the Quran, and it names a distance by what it costs rather than by how far it is. The classical commentators gloss it with words for hardship rather than for length, and note that the ayah identifies the difficulty as the deciding factor before anyone else does.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a decision from the account a person gives of it, and puts the weight on the second. Staying behind is described almost neutrally, as a calculation anyone might make; what is condemned is the oath sworn over it afterwards. That places the moral centre in what someone says about what they did, which is a claim about where self-deception actually begins.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with the question of why permission was granted before the truthful became clear.
Describes oaths taken as a shield by people whose words do not match them.
Addresses those who swear their strongest oaths that they would go out if commanded.

studies.applyIt: Catch one explanation you gave this week that was true in its words and false in its shape. You do not need to correct it to anybody. Just write the actual reason next to the given one and read the two together. The passage is not about the choice. It is about the sentence that came afterwards.

studies.title: The Pardon Comes First
studies.meaning: The pardon arrives before the question, and that ordering is the whole structure of the ayah. God has pardoned you, and then: why did you grant them leave before it had become clear to you who was truthful and who was lying. Something is being corrected, and the correction is bracketed by forgiveness on the way in. Commentators discuss whether the opening softens a reproach or simply states a mercy first.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) concerning permissions granted to men who asked to be excused from the march north. The commentators read the passage as saying that granting leave removed a moment in which the excuses would have shown themselves for what they were. The ayat that follow describe those excuses at length.

keyTerms.note: This exact phrase occurs only once in the Quran. The verb means to efface something rather than merely to overlook it, and the commentaries discuss at length why the pardon precedes the question instead of following it.
The verb for granting leave, built on the root for hearing. What is being questioned is an act of kindness rather than a fault, which is what makes this correction unusual among the Quran's.
A reflexive verb meaning to become distinct of its own accord. It names something that would have emerged if left alone, rather than an inquiry that anyone would have had to conduct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader who refused a request for leave in that society made an enemy, and one who granted every request lost his expedition. Every commander in Arabia navigated that, and the usual solution was to let a man state his excuse publicly so his own people could judge it. What is described here is the cost of sparing someone that hearing, which any leader would recognise.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that opens this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The classical commentaries devote considerable attention to the fact that a pardon is stated before the question that follows it rather than after, and several treat the ordering itself as the passage's most striking feature.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows a correction given inside an established relationship rather than handed down as a judgement upon one. Nothing is left at stake in the pardon; it is stated first so that the question can be heard as a question. It also treats an excess of kindness as something that can go wrong, which is a harder observation than any warning against harshness.

crossReferences.why: Continues the point, describing who does and who does not ask to be excused.
Contains another correction addressed to the Prophet, phrased in an entirely different manner.
Attributes his gentleness with people to God's mercy, describing the same disposition at work.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time your kindness let someone avoid a conversation they needed to have. Not a failure of nerve, a genuine kindness with a cost attached. Name one, without deciding you were wrong. The pardon here comes first precisely so that the question can be looked at before a defence goes up around it.

studies.title: They Do Not Ask To Be Excused
studies.meaning: The statement is made from the other direction. Those who believe in God and the last day do not come asking to be let off striving with their wealth and their persons. Nothing is said about what they do; the sign given is what they do not do. The clause then closes on knowledge rather than reward, so the test described is one that nobody administers and nobody sees applied.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the correction about permissions granted. The commentators read this ayah and the next as a pair, one describing who does not ask and the other who does. The setting is the march north, when requests to be excused were arriving and being decided one at a time, and the surah describes the pattern behind them rather than judging particular cases.

keyTerms.gloss: they do not ask your leave
keyTerms.note: The verb of requesting permission, built on the root for hearing. Putting it in the negative makes an absence into the evidence, which is a difficult kind of sign to counterfeit in either direction.
This pairing appears four times in this surah alone, more than in any other. Here it names what the exemption would have been from, so a request is measured against a specific cost.

keyTerms.gloss: aware of those who guard themselves
keyTerms.note: The clause ends with knowledge rather than with recompense. It removes any need for the pattern just described to be checked by anyone, which keeps it from becoming a test of membership.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Requests to be excused were made in person and heard by others. A man came, stated his difficulty, and the answer was given in front of whoever happened to be standing there. There was no form to fill in and no private channel. That made the act of asking itself visible, and a man's neighbours knew who had come forward and exactly what he had said.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming wealth and person together occurs seven times in the Quran, and four of those are in this surah, more than anywhere else. Three of the four fall inside this section on the march north, so a single measure of commitment is applied again and again within a few pages of text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a disposition by an absence rather than by an act, and that changes what can be observed. An absence cannot be performed for an audience and cannot be counted up. It places the sign beyond the reach of both display and administration. And by closing on God's awareness, the ayah declines to hand anybody a criterion for sorting other people with.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing from the other side, describing who does come asking to be excused.
Describes believers who do not leave a gathering without asking, a request running the opposite way.
Names belief without doubt and striving with wealth and person as the mark of the truthful.

studies.applyIt: Watch what you ask to be let out of this week. Not what you take on, what you seek release from. Write down one request you made or nearly made, and look at the reason underneath it. This ayah reads a person by their exemptions, which is a measurement most of us have never turned on ourselves.

studies.title: Wavering Inside Their Doubt
studies.meaning: The other half of the pair, and the description moves inward. Those who ask to be excused are the ones whose hearts have fallen into doubt, and the closing word says what doubt does to a person: they go back and forth inside it. Not resolving, not deciding, not leaving. The image is motion without direction, offered as a condition rather than delivered as a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, paired with the ayah before it. The commentators read the two together as one statement about the pattern of requests during preparations for the march north. This ayah names doubt rather than fear as what lies underneath, which is a specific diagnosis, and the surah develops it through the several ayat that follow.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the root for uncertainty and suspicion. The form suggests something the hearts fell into rather than a position anyone adopted, so doubt is described as a condition that arrives.
The noun from the same root, repeated within one sentence. Doubt is named twice in a single line, once as what happened to them and once as the space they are now moving about inside.

keyTerms.gloss: they waver, go back and forth
keyTerms.note: A verb of repeated return, used of something oscillating rather than travelling. It occurs only here in the Quran and pictures movement that covers no ground at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller who set out, turned back, and set out again was a familiar figure and a costly one. Caravans left on a schedule because water and pasture along a route were timed to the season, so a man who could not commit missed the window entirely and stayed home by default. The picture of going back and forth carried that association immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing what doubt does here occurs only once in the whole Quran. It is built on the root for returning, doubled inside the word itself, so the form of the term performs the state it names before the sentence has explained anything about it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the trouble in doubt rather than in cowardice, which is at once more sympathetic and more serious. Fear can be met with resolve; doubt cannot, because there is nothing settled for resolve to act upon. Describing the condition as movement inside a space also refuses to treat it as fixed, which leaves it as something that could still come to an end.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half of the pair, describing those who never ask to be excused.
Describes people wavering between two sides and belonging fully to neither of them.
Names a sickness in the heart and says it was increased, in similar diagnostic language.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you have made and unmade several times this month. Do not decide it today. Write down instead what you would need to know for it to be settled, and whether that knowledge exists at all. Most wavering is not weakness; it is a question being put to a situation that cannot answer it.

studies.title: Intention Read From Preparation
studies.meaning: The reasoning starts from evidence anyone could have seen. Had they intended to go out, they would have made preparation for it, and no preparation was made. Intention is read from equipment rather than from statements. Then the sentence turns and says something harder: God disliked their setting out and slowed them, and a voice said sit with those who sit. The withholding is described from both sides at once.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, within the section on the march north. The commentators note that preparations for that expedition were public and lengthy, involving mounts, provisions and water for a long desert route, so an absence of preparation was visible to everyone. They discuss the second half of the ayah, where the holding back is attributed to God, alongside other passages about human intention.

keyTerms.note: The verb and its object come from a single root, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis. The doubling insists on the visibility of preparing, which is exactly what the argument rests on.
A noun from a verb meaning to be sent forth or raised up. It occurs only once in the Quran and names the act of getting moving rather than the journey that would follow.
A verb meaning to slow or discourage rather than to prevent outright. Commentators note that it describes weight added to a reluctance already present rather than force applied against a will.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Preparing for a long march took weeks and could not be hidden. Camels were fattened and rested, waterskins checked and re-sealed, dates and barley bought in quantity, and a whole household knew about it. Neighbours could tell who was going simply by walking past a courtyard. Saying you intended to travel while making no preparation was not a claim anyone could sustain.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for their setting out occurs only once in the Quran, and it comes from the root that elsewhere describes the raising of the dead. The commentators note the choice: the passage speaks of getting a reluctant body moving using the same verb the Quran uses for bodies brought out of the earth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reads an intention from its traces, which is a claim about how intentions work: they leave evidence behind them, and an absence of evidence is itself evidence. It then attributes the holding back to God without removing the reluctance from the people. Both are stated, and the commentators keep both, which is characteristic of how the Quran handles a will inside a larger one.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same reluctance from outside, as a body growing heavy toward the ground.
Says obedience and a fitting word would have been better for them than what they did.
Instructs travellers to take provision, treating preparation as part of the undertaking itself.

studies.applyIt: Check your calendar against your stated intentions. Whatever you say you are going to do, look for the preparation: time blocked out, money set aside, a message actually sent. Where there is none, the intention is a wish, and knowing that is more useful than renewing it. Prepare one small piece of it today instead.

studies.title: Among You Are Listeners
studies.meaning: The claim is counterintuitive and the passage makes it plainly: their absence was better than their presence. Had they gone out, they would have added only disorder and hurried about among the ranks looking to unsettle them. Then a clause turns on the community itself: among you are people who listen to them eagerly. The vulnerability is named as internal, which is the sharper half of the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, during preparation for the march north. The commentators read this ayah as explaining the one before it, since the holding back described there is here given a reason. The surah is unusually direct about internal division in this section, addressing a community that had grown quickly and contained people whose commitments were genuinely mixed.

keyTerms.note: A word for confusion of mind and for the spoiling of something sound. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 3:118, and both times of harm introduced into a group from close quarters.
From a verb used of a camel quickening its pace. It occurs only once in the Quran and pictures rapid movement between people rather than a fixed position taken up somewhere.
An intensive form meaning those who listen a great deal. The Quran does not say they agree with what they hear; it says they listen, which places the danger in an audience rather than a message.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An army on the march was a rumour engine. Men walked for hours with nothing to do but talk, camped in groups at night, and had no way to check anything they heard until it was all over. One well-placed story about the water ahead, or about who was really in command, could empty a camp before morning. Commanders managed talk as carefully as supplies.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the harm they would have added occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 3:118, and in both places it describes damage introduced into a community by people already inside it or standing close to it. The rare word is reserved for that particular kind of injury and no other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says a group can be strengthened by a subtraction, which is an uncomfortable claim about belonging. It also refuses to put all the fault outside: the ones who listen are addressed in the same sentence as the ones who talk. That divides the responsibility, and it names the receptive ear rather than the persuasive tongue as the thing that makes damage possible.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same rare word for harm caused by taking intimates from outside the community.
Requires verification when news arrives, addressing the listening rather than the telling.
Asks why believers did not think well of one another when a rumour reached them.

studies.applyIt: This ayah addresses the listeners, not only the talkers. Notice one piece of information you passed on this week without checking it. Go back to whoever you told and say you do not actually know whether it was true. The correction is small and slightly humiliating, which is roughly what the passage is describing.

studies.title: Until The Truth Came
studies.meaning: A long record is compressed into one sentence. They sought to unsettle things before this, and they turned matters over and over against you, until the truth came and God's command showed itself, and they disliked it. The clause ends with an arrival rather than a defeat. What is described is a long stretch of pressure followed by a change that nobody named in the sentence brought about.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, looking back across the whole Medinan period. The commentators connect the plotting mentioned here to episodes in earlier years, including moments when the community was under direct threat, and they treat the ayah as summarising rather than reporting one event. Its placement is deliberate: the summary is offered while a difficult expedition is being prepared.

keyTerms.gloss: they turned matters over against you
keyTerms.note: The verb means to overturn or to keep flipping something. Applied to affairs it pictures schemes examined from every side, and commentators read it of persistent contrivance rather than a single plan.
The verb is simple arrival. Nothing in the sentence achieves it; the truth is described as showing up, which is the grammar the passage chooses for its turning point.
The clause ends on their feeling rather than on their defeat. The Quran uses this construction repeatedly to note that an outcome arrived without the agreement of the people it happened to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Political pressure in Medina worked through talk, marriage, debt and old alliances rather than through open force. A man could weaken a rival for years without a single confrontation, by placing a rumour, calling in an obligation, or reviving a feud from the previous generation. Everyone in the town could name who was doing it, and everyone waited to see how long it would last.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the middle of three consecutive ayat that each use the same word for discord and sedition, at 9:47, 9:48 and 9:49. Three occurrences within three ayat is dense even for the Quran, and the third turns the word back on a man who had used it to ask for an exemption.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats an outcome as an arrival rather than a victory. Nothing in the sentence claims that anyone outmanoeuvred anyone; the truth came, and the matter changed. That takes the account out of the register of strategy and puts it in the register of endurance. The final clause then declines to describe anybody as persuaded, which keeps the change external to their consent.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same people's likely conduct on the march, using the same word for discord.
States that truth has come and falsehood has vanished, in the same grammar of arrival.
Describes an earlier plot and the planning that met it, from the same period.

studies.applyIt: Think of a pressure that has been on you long enough that you have stopped expecting it to end. Write down what would actually have to change for it to be over, then notice how much of that list is outside your hands. This ayah's account of the turning point credits nobody on the field with arranging it.

studies.title: Do Not Put Me To The Test
studies.meaning: A request is quoted and it is beautifully phrased: excuse me, and do not put me to the test. The words are pious and the ask is exemption. The reply is one turn of the same word back on the speaker: into the test they have already fallen. Nothing about his sincerity is investigated. The sentence works entirely by noticing that his own vocabulary has answered him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the requests to be excused from the march north. The classical sources preserve an account of who spoke this line and what he claimed to be afraid of, with some variation in the details. They agree on the structure of the reply, which turns the requester's own chosen word back against his request rather than disputing his reason.

keyTerms.note: The same verb of permission that runs through this whole short section. The request is formally correct, which is part of what the passage is showing: nothing in the wording itself gives it away.
From a root for testing metal by fire, extended to any severe trial and also to discord. The speaker picks a religious word for what he wants to avoid, and the reply takes hold of that word.
The ordinary verb for falling down, in the past tense. The thing he asks to be spared is described as already having happened, so the exemption arrives too late by its own terms.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society without written applications, an excuse was a short speech made in front of others, and its wording mattered as much as its content. Men learned the phrases that worked. A request framed in religious language was hard to refuse publicly without appearing to doubt the speaker. This ayah quotes one such phrase exactly and answers it without disputing a single word.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this man uses for the trial he wants to avoid appears in the two ayat immediately before this one as well, at 9:47 and 9:48, where it names the discord the same group would have caused. By the time he reaches for it, the surah has already settled what the word means here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not accuse the speaker of lying. It observes that his request describes his situation more accurately than he means it to, which is a different and more unsettling kind of exposure. That method assumes people mostly tell the truth about themselves in the vocabulary they reach for, and it puts the weight on listening carefully rather than on suspecting.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the discord this group would have introduced among the ranks.
Poses testing as the expected condition rather than as something to be excused from.
States that people may dislike what is good for them, which answers the request directly.

studies.applyIt: Listen to the words you choose for what you are avoiding. If you find yourself using a serious word, about capacity or protecting yourself, for something you simply do not want to do, that is worth a minute of honesty. The passage does not argue with the reason. It listens to the word and lets it speak.

studies.title: What Their Faces Do First
studies.meaning: Two reactions are set against each other and both are involuntary. Good reaches you and it grieves them; a hardship strikes and they say we took our precautions in advance, and they walk away pleased. The passage describes no argument and no plot. It describes what a person feels when somebody else's news arrives, and it treats that as the most reliable evidence available about them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, in the section on those who stayed behind from the march north. The commentators read this ayah as describing a settled disposition rather than one episode, and they note that the surah moves here from what people did to how they responded to events they had no part in. The following ayah supplies the answer the community is told to give.

keyTerms.note: The verb for causing distress, taking good news as its subject. The construction makes another person's fortune the active thing and these listeners the passive ones, which is precisely how the feeling arrives.
Literally, we took our matter in hand. It is what a person says when a risk they declined turns out badly for others, and it converts a failure to take part into foresight.
The Quran uses this word both for legitimate joy and for a self-satisfied gladness. Here it closes the sentence, so the departure is described entirely by the mood of the one leaving.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News of an expedition came back in fragments over several days: a rider ahead of the column, then travellers, then the returning men themselves. In that gap everyone in Medina had time to arrange their face. The people described here had declined to go, and each report from the north either justified or embarrassed that decision in front of their neighbours.
studies.didYouKnow: The two halves of this ayah are exactly symmetrical in Arabic. The same verb of striking introduces both the good and the calamity, with only the object changed between them. The construction sets one man's fortune and misfortune in identical frames, so the whole difference the ayah reports lies in the reaction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes an involuntary reaction as evidence, which raises the standard considerably. A person can control what they do about someone else's good fortune; what they feel in the first second is much harder to arrange. By recording that instead of any action, the ayah suggests the interior is where the account is kept, and that it is legible from outside more often than people assume.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same pair of reactions to another community's good and ill fortune.
Gives the answer the community is instructed to make to this whole attitude.
Discusses the habit of assigning good and evil fortune to different sources.

studies.applyIt: Catch the first half-second when you hear that someone you know has done well. Not what you say next, which you can manage. What arrived before that. You do not have to fix it. Noticing it accurately, once, does more than a month of deciding to be pleased for people.

studies.title: Only What Is Written For Us
studies.meaning: The reply is short and its grammar does the work. Nothing reaches us except what God has written for us, with the preposition meaning for rather than against, so even hardship is placed on the side of what is given. Then a title, our guardian, and finally an instruction phrased in the third person rather than the second, which lets the sentence state a general rule instead of pressing a demand on the person hearing it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage about people who took satisfaction in setbacks falling on the community while keeping clear of anything costly themselves. This is the answer the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is told to give them. The commentators read it as addressing an attitude rather than an event, and note that the reply concedes nothing about whether the setbacks were real.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something hitting its target, used of arrows and of rain. It presents events as arriving with an aim rather than as accidents, which is why the sentence can go on to name who sent them.

The preposition here means for rather than upon. Commentators note the choice: what is written is presented as assigned in a person’s favour, which places even difficulty inside the category of what is given.
A word from the vocabulary of protection and clientage, used of the person responsible for someone with no other backing. It carries obligation rather than merely power, which is why it reassures.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clientage was a formal institution in Arabia. A person without a tribe attached themselves to a patron who guaranteed their safety and answered for their wrongs, and the relationship was public and binding. Naming God with that title was legally precise language rather than sentiment: it claimed a protector who could be called on and who had accepted the obligation.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction closing the ayah is phrased in the third person, telling believers what believers should do rather than addressing them directly. Arabic uses that form for stating a norm, and the Quran uses it sparingly. Here it lets a reply given to opponents double as a rule the community could take away from the exchange.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage neither denies hardship nor explains it. It relocates authorship, which is a different move: the question of why something happened is set aside for the question of whose it is. Naming God as guardian then adds obligation to power, so the claim is not merely that He controls events but that He has taken responsibility for the people inside them. Reliance follows as the reasonable response.

crossReferences.why: States that no misfortune occurs except as already recorded before it happens.
Adds that whoever believes has their heart guided through the misfortune.
Records the same reliance stated in the community's own words under threat.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you are most afraid will happen and write one sentence describing it, then add the words that this too would be written for you rather than against you. You are not deciding it will not happen. You are testing whether the sentence changes anything, which is the only way to find out.

studies.title: One Of The Two Good Ends
studies.meaning: A reply is put in the community's mouth and it opens as a question. Are you waiting for anything to reach us except one of the two best outcomes. The phrase is a dual: two goods, and either counts. Then the direction reverses and the passage turns to spending, saying that what is given willingly or unwillingly will not be accepted. The reply and its hard edge arrive together.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the reaction described in the ayah before. The commentators identify the two goods as prevailing or the reward of one who falls in the attempt, and they read the reply as addressed to people who assumed that hardship would settle the argument for them. The second of these two ayat turns to contributions, a subject the surah returns to repeatedly here.

keyTerms.note: A dual form of the word for the finest, occurring only once in the Quran. Arabic marks pairs with their own grammatical form, so the phrase says two and exactly two, both of them good.
The verb of awaiting an outcome. It occurs four times across this short passage with the subject changing each time, so both sides are described as waiting and only the expectation differs.
A pair covering both ends of a range, the same construction the surah uses for light and heavy. Here it closes off the possibility that the manner of giving could change the outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A campaign's result was normally binary in that world: you came back with something or you did not come back at all. Families waited for the column to appear on the horizon and counted heads as it arrived. The reply quoted here rearranges that arithmetic without denying it, spoken in a town where everyone present had waited for a returning party at least once.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the two best outcomes occurs only once in the Quran, and it is grammatically a dual, a form Arabic reserves for exactly two things. The verb for waiting then appears four times within the same short passage, applied to both sides in turn, so the exchange is constructed as a mirror.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes the leverage that misfortune usually carries. If both possible outcomes are named as good, the person waiting for the bad one has nothing left to wait for, and the argument they expected to win cannot be had at all. The second ayah then withholds acceptance from spending done without conviction, so the same act can be worth nothing depending on what stands behind it.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the first half of the answer, that nothing reaches us except what God has written.
Names the same two outcomes, forgiveness and mercy or being gathered to God.
Describes charity emptied by what accompanies it, the principle behind the second ayah here.

studies.applyIt: Name the outcome you are dreading and ask whether there is a version of it you could live with well. Not a silver lining. An honest second good end. If you can find one, the waiting changes shape, and if you cannot, you have learned something specific about what you are actually afraid of.

studies.title: Coming To Prayer Heavily
studies.meaning: The question left open by the previous ayah is answered structurally. What prevents their contributions being accepted is nothing but three things, listed as a single condition. They rejected God and His Messenger; they do not come to the prayer except heavily; and they do not spend except unwillingly. The two habits are faulted in exactly the same way, by the manner in which each is performed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, explaining the statement in the ayah before. The commentators note that the passage does not say the contributions were small or the prayers missed. Both were being made. What is described is how, and the surah applies this to a specific group during a period when attendance and contribution were both highly visible within the community.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective for sluggishness. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 4:142, and in both places it describes standing for prayer, which is the only act it is ever used of.
The active participle of the verb to dislike. Paired with the previous word it forms a matching structure, so the two acts are faulted identically rather than for different reasons.
The noun from the verb for spending out. It names the amounts given rather than the giving, which sharpens the point: the money was real and the passage still speaks of it as unaccepted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both acts named here were performed in public. The prayer gathered the town several times a day, and everyone could see who arrived early, who arrived at the last moment, and who left first. Contributions were carried in and set down in front of others. In a settlement that size, the manner of doing either was as visible as the doing itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for coming to prayer heavily occurs only twice in the Quran, here and at 4:142, and in both places it describes the same act. Standing for prayer is the only thing the Quran ever calls doing sluggishly, which makes the pairing across the two passages deliberate rather than incidental.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats an act and its manner as inseparable, so a completed act can still fail to count. That is a demanding standard, and it cuts against the intuition that at least the outward performance is safe ground. The surah applies it here to one group in a particular crisis, but the criterion it names, whether a thing is done unwillingly, is stated in general terms.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for standing to prayer heavily, in a closely parallel description.
Describes charity destroyed by what is done alongside it rather than by its amount.
Names those who are heedless of their prayer while still performing it.

studies.applyIt: Pick the obligation you meet most reluctantly and do it once this week with your full attention, from beginning to end. Same act, same amount of time. The ayah is not asking for more of anything; it is describing a difference in how, and that difference is easier to feel from inside than to argue about.

studies.title: Let It Not Impress You
studies.meaning: The instruction concerns how to see rather than what to do. Let neither their wealth nor their children impress you. Then comes the reason, which inverts what such things ordinarily mean: God intends to punish them through these very things in this life, and that their souls should leave while they are still in that state. The blessing and the instrument are named as the same objects.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the ayat about those who stayed behind. The commentators read the passage as addressing an impression rather than disputing a fact, since the wealth and the children were real enough. The ayah appears twice in this surah in nearly identical wording, here and at 9:85, which the commentaries treat as an emphasis characteristic of this section.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used at 9:25 of numbers impressing an army before a reversal. The surah applies it twice to being struck by a quantity, once to one's own and once to somebody else's.
The pronoun points back to the wealth and children. What was listed as blessing becomes the instrument, so nothing is taken away from them and nothing new is added.
A verb used of a soul leaving with difficulty, carrying a sense of being forced out. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah and both times inside this same sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth and sons were the two visible measures of a man's position. Sons meant labour, protection, and a name that continued; wealth meant standing in any negotiation. Nobody in that society looked at a prosperous household full of children and saw anything but success. This instruction asks the listener to interrupt a judgement everyone around them made automatically.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah appears twice in the surah in almost identical words, here and again at 9:85, differing only in a few particles. The surah repeats very little else at that length, and the commentators treat the repetition as marking the passage's weight within the section on those who stayed behind.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the appearance of a blessing from what it is doing. The same objects can be given and can be the means of a loss, which means the outward state of a life is not evidence about it either way. That denies the reader a shortcut in both directions: prosperity proves nothing, and hardship proves nothing either, and the judgement stays suspended.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this ayah almost word for word later in the same section of the surah.
Asks whether the wealth and sons given to people are a hastening of good for them.
Warns that a respite granted to some is not the good they take it to be.

studies.applyIt: Take one person whose life you have quietly judged by its visible results, in either direction. Set the judgement down for a week. Not to think better of them, and not worse. To stop using the outside as evidence, and to notice how often you had been doing that without ever deciding to.

studies.title: A Refuge, A Cave, A Hole
studies.meaning: An oath is quoted and denied in the same breath: they swear by God that they belong with you, and they do not. Then the reason is given in one word whose sense the commentators discuss, reading it either as fear or as division. The second ayah settles it with an image. Given a refuge, a cave, or any hole to squeeze into, they would bolt for it, running past stopping.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, in the section on those who remained behind from the march north. The commentators read the two ayat together, the second illustrating the word at the end of the first. The oath being quoted was a real social act with weight behind it, which is why the passage records it before answering rather than dismissing the claim outright.

keyTerms.gloss: they are afraid, they are divided
keyTerms.note: From a root that gives both fear and separation. Commentators record both readings, and the ayah that follows, with its image of men bolting for a hole, is usually cited to settle it toward fear.

keyTerms.gloss: a refuge, a place to flee
keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to take shelter. It occurs only once in the Quran and heads a list of three hiding places that descends from the respectable to the undignified.
A verb used of a horse that has taken the bit and cannot be turned. It occurs only once in the Quran and describes a body running past the point where anyone could stop it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The three places named describe an actual landscape. A refuge might be a walled enclosure or an allied camp; caves pitted the hills around Medina and men used them to hide livestock; and the last word covers any burrow a person could force themselves into. The list descends from what a man would admit to afterwards to what he would never mention again.
studies.didYouKnow: All three hiding places named in the second of these ayat are words that occur only once each in the Quran, and the verb for bolting toward them is unique to this passage as well. Four rare words inside a single short ayah is unusual, and the commentaries take each of them in turn.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets an oath and a body against each other and lets the body decide. A person can swear sincerely and still be described by what they would do if a door opened, which is a claim about where someone's real position sits. It also treats the fear itself as diagnostic rather than blameworthy, since what it reveals is what remains when a stated belonging is subtracted.

crossReferences.why: Records a similar oath of belonging and answers it in almost identical terms.
Describes people who withhold, whose eyes roll with fear when danger arrives.
Describes those who fear people as they should fear God, or even more.

studies.applyIt: Ask where you would go if the thing you are committed to became genuinely costly tomorrow. Answer honestly and privately: the exit you would take, and how fast. You are not deciding anything by answering. You are finding out whether the commitment already has an escape route scouted, which most of them quietly do.

studies.title: Pleased When They Are Given
studies.meaning: The complaint is about distribution, and the passage exposes its mechanism in one sentence. Some of them find fault with you concerning the charities; if they are given from them they are pleased, and if they are not, they are immediately resentful. The criticism is dressed as principle and it moves with the payment. Nothing further needs saying about it, and the ayah says nothing further.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators place these ayat among those concerning the distribution of collected charity, which the surah sets out in detail two ayat later. Complaints about who received what were being made openly in the town, and the passage answers them by describing when they arose rather than by defending any particular allocation.

keyTerms.gloss: finds fault with you, taunts you
