keyTerms.note: A verb for criticism made by gesture or under the breath rather than openly. The verb occurs twice in this surah, here and again at 9:79, and the same root gives the second word of surah 104.
The verb for being satisfied, from the same root as the word used earlier in the surah for God's acceptance. Here it names a satisfaction that arrives together with a payment.
The verb for indignant displeasure, set directly opposite the previous word. The two sit in matching clauses, so the swing between them is the entire content of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Collected charity arrived as physical goods: animals, grain, dates, sometimes coin, brought in from surrounding tribes and distributed in the open. Everyone could see the pile and everyone could see who left with what. In a settlement that size, distribution was the most scrutinised act any leader performed, and complaints about it were the ordinary currency of the town.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for finding fault names criticism made by a gesture, a look or a muttered remark rather than by open objection. The same root supplies the second word of surah 104, which opens with a warning to every backbiter, so the Quran keeps this particular kind of criticism in a category of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a moral complaint by timing it. If an objection appears only when a person is left out and disappears the moment they are included, then the objection was never about the principle. That test is transferable and slightly brutal, and it is offered without any defence of the distribution itself, which the surah leaves for two ayat later.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the categories among whom the collected charity is distributed, two ayat later.
Opens with a warning against the muttered kind of criticism this verb names.
Addresses finding fault with one another, using the same root for the act.

studies.applyIt: Test one of your own objections by timing. Think of something you have criticised, and ask whether you would still be criticising it if you had been included, chosen or paid. If the answer is no, the objection may still be correct, but it is not why you made it, and knowing that changes how you make it next time.

studies.title: God Is Enough For Us
studies.meaning: The sentence is a wish rather than a statement, and it is deliberately left unfinished. If only they had been content with what God and His Messenger gave them, and had said: God is enough for us, God will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. A whole reply is scripted for them, words they might have spoken. What would have followed is never stated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the complaint about how collected charity was distributed. The commentators read this ayah as supplying what the complainers could have said instead. Distribution was made in public at a moment when contributions had been called for repeatedly, so dissatisfaction with a share was a live and audible matter throughout the town.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs twice in the Quran. The other place is 3:173, where it is spoken by people warned that a large force had gathered, so the same words serve a battlefield and a disappointing share.
An active participle from a verb meaning to want something keenly. The construction directs the wanting toward God rather than removing it, so what is offered here is not the absence of desire.
The word means overflow beyond what is owed. Putting it in the future tense makes the sentence an expectation rather than a resignation, which is what separates it from simply giving up.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shares were allotted publicly and remembered exactly. In a society where a man's portion from a distribution was seen by everyone standing there, receiving less than expected was a matter of standing as much as of goods. Poetry from the period is full of complaints about allotment. The sentence supplied here would have been spoken in front of the same crowd.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this ayah wishes they had spoken, that God is enough for us, appears in only one other place in the Quran, at 3:173, where it is said by people told that a large force had gathered against them. The same four words answer a battlefield in one place and a disappointing share in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not ask for indifference. The sentence it supplies contains an expectation of more, stated openly, alongside a declaration that what has already arrived is sufficient. Holding both at once is the exact posture being described. Contentment in this sense is not the end of wanting but a wanting that has been given a direction.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same declaration, spoken by people facing a gathered force rather than a small share.
Describes the complaint about distribution that this ayah answers with a different sentence.
Warns against straining the eyes toward what others have been given to enjoy.

studies.applyIt: Write the sentence this ayah supplies, in your own words, about the specific thing you feel short-changed on. It has two halves: this is enough, and more may come. Say both. Most disappointment is that sentence with one half missing, and which half is missing tells you something.

studies.title: Eight Named Categories
studies.meaning: Eight categories are listed and the list is closed by a restrictive particle at its head: the charities are only for these. The poor, the destitute, those employed to collect them, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, the freeing of necks, the indebted, the path of God, and the traveller cut off. It is then called an obligation from God, which puts the list beyond anyone's discretion.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, two ayat after the complaints about distribution. The commentators read the list as the answer to those complaints: a fixed set replaces discretion entirely. They discuss each category at length and differ over the scope of several, particularly the reconciling of hearts and the path of God, recording the range of readings without settling them.

keyTerms.note: A word for something apportioned and settled. It occurs five times in the Quran, four of them about marriage payments and inheritance shares, and only here of charity, which places it among fixed entitlements.

The preposition changes for this category and two others, reading in rather than for. Commentators note the shift and read those three as purposes to be spent on rather than people to be handed money.
From a verb meaning to be liable for a loss. It occurs only once in the Quran, and commentators discuss whether it covers debts taken on for oneself and debts assumed to settle disputes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in that economy could take a household apart. A bad season, a lost caravan, or compensation owed after an accident could put a man into obligations he would never clear, and his family into service to clear them. Naming the indebted as a category meant the collection was expected to reach people who did not look poor and would never have asked.
studies.didYouKnow: The word calling this an obligation occurs five times in the Quran. Four of those concern marriage payments and inheritance shares, fixed amounts that cannot be adjusted by whoever is handling them, and this is the only place it is applied to charity, which sets the eight categories in that same class of settled entitlement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage converts a discretionary generosity into a set of entitlements. Once the categories are fixed, whoever distributes has no standing to be thanked, and whoever receives is not accepting a favour. That changes the relation between the two, which the complaint two ayat earlier had made necessary. It also names purposes alongside people, so the collection is repair as well as relief.

crossReferences.why: Records the complaints about distribution that this fixed list answers directly.
Names several of the same recipients as the substance of righteousness rather than its direction.
Explains that wealth should not circulate only among the rich among you.

studies.applyIt: Give something this week to a category rather than to a person you know. Pick one of the eight with an equivalent where you live: a debtor, a stranded traveller, someone doing the work of collection. The point is the shift from choosing a face to answering a need that was named before you arrived.

studies.title: An Ear Of Good For You
studies.meaning: An insult is quoted and then reversed by being accepted. They say he is all ears, meaning he believes whatever he is told. The reply keeps the word and adds one thing to it: an ear of good for you. Listening is not denied, it is reclassified. Then the sentence unfolds what the listening consists of: he trusts God, he trusts the believers, and he is a mercy to those among you who believe.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the ayat describing those who stayed behind from the march north. The commentators explain the taunt as mockery of a leader who heard everyone out, including people whose excuses were not sincere. The reply is addressed to the mockers rather than to the community, and it defends the practice rather than denying that it happened.

keyTerms.note: The word for the organ, applied to a person. The reply repeats it immediately and attaches good to it, so the same term stands twice in one sentence, first as an insult and then as a description.

The verb of believing takes an unusual preposition here, shifting its sense from believing in to believing for, meaning trusting. Commentators note the construction as deliberate rather than incidental.
A noun rather than an adjective, so the sentence says he is mercy rather than merciful. The Quran uses the same construction of him at 21:107, addressed there to all the worlds.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A chief who listened to everyone was making a costly choice. In a society of competing claims, hearing every petitioner meant hours lost, and it meant liars got their hearing too. The alternative was a leader surrounded by intermediaries, which is what most powerful men in that world had. Being called all ears was a comment on a policy anyone could observe.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply keeps the insulting word instead of replacing it, using it twice in a single sentence and adding one genitive that turns it around. The classical commentaries treat this reversal, rather than any counter-argument, as the answer the ayah is giving to the taunt it quotes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats openness to being deceived as a cost worth paying. It never claims the listening was discerning; it claims it was good for the people being listened to, including the ones abusing it. That locates the value of an attentive ear in what it does for others rather than in its accuracy, which is an unusual way to defend a practice.

crossReferences.why: Names him a mercy for all the worlds, using the same noun rather than an adjective.
Says that had he been harsh they would have scattered from around him.
Describes his concern for the people and his gentleness toward the believers.

studies.applyIt: Think of the trait people tease you for that is actually a decision: too soft, too slow, too willing to hear people out. Do not defend it this week. Just check whether it is doing the good you intended, for the people you intended it for. That is the only question the reply here actually answers.

studies.title: Sworn To Please You
studies.meaning: The observation is about direction rather than about truthfulness. They swear to you by God in order to please you. The oath is aimed at an audience, and the audience is the wrong one. The correction is then framed as a comparison of claims: God and His Messenger have more right to be pleased, if they are believers. The conditional at the end is where the sentence puts its weight.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the excuses offered after the march north. The commentators note that oaths sworn to the community were being used to settle a social matter rather than a religious one, and that the ayah does not dispute the content of any particular oath. The surrounding ayat describe the same group in similar terms, repeatedly by who they are addressing.

keyTerms.note: The purpose clause is the whole point of the sentence. It names the target of the act rather than its truth, which is why the correction that follows concerns direction and not honesty.
A comparative built on the word for truth and right. The Quran uses it to rank two claims rather than to cancel one, so the community's claim is not denied here, only placed second.
A conditional closing the sentence rather than opening it. It leaves the ranking resting on something the listener holds, so the correction only reaches a person who already accepts the premise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath sworn by God was the strongest instrument a person had, and it was used constantly in ordinary business: to close a sale, to end a dispute, to settle a doubt about where someone had been the night before. That everyday use is what the passage is describing. The oath was doing social work and doing it well, which is precisely the difficulty.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for pleasing occurs twice in this short ayah, once with the community as its object and once with God, setting the two side by side inside one sentence. The same root runs through this whole passage: at 9:58 and 9:59 of people pleased with a share, and at 9:72 of acceptance from God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage evaluates an act by its intended audience rather than by its content. An oath can be entirely true and still be misdirected, which means sincerity here is not only a matter of matching words to facts. It concerns who the words are for. The closing conditional then makes the correction internal, reaching only someone who already grants what it assumes.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root for being pleased, there about a share received rather than a person addressed.
Concerns fearing people when God has more right to be feared, in the same comparative form.
Describes giving done to be seen by people, the same misdirection appearing in another act.

studies.applyIt: Take something you did well this week and ask who you were doing it for. Not whether it was good, it may have been excellent. Just the audience. If you can name the person whose approval you were tracking, you have found what this ayah points at, and you can leave it there for now.

studies.title: Do They Not Already Know
studies.meaning: The sentence opens as a question about knowledge rather than about conduct. Do they not know. What follows is presented as already available rather than newly disclosed: whoever sets himself against God and His Messenger has the fire. The verb for that opposition is built on the word for a boundary, so it pictures a person standing deliberately on the far side of a line. The outcome is then named as disgrace.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, in the section on those who swore oaths to the community after staying behind. The commentators read the question as rhetorical: the information was public and had been repeated many times. The ayah sits among descriptions of behaviour rather than of doctrine, which is how the surah joins what people know to what they nevertheless do.

keyTerms.note: A question expecting the answer yes. The Quran uses this construction where information is not what is lacking, which places the failure between knowing something and letting it govern anything.
Built on the word for a limit or boundary. It pictures taking up a position on the far side of a line rather than fighting across it, and this form occurs only once in the Quran.
The noun names public humiliation rather than pain. Choosing it as the summary word makes exposure the central feature, which suits a surah preoccupied with things being brought into the open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disgrace was the most feared social outcome in that world, and it was administered by memory. A man shamed publicly carried it into every negotiation for the rest of his life, and his sons carried it after him. Poets built reputations by inflicting it. Naming disgrace rather than pain as the summary uses the vocabulary the audience feared most.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for opposition here occurs in this form only once in the Quran, and it is built on the ordinary word for a boundary or limit. The image is spatial rather than martial: someone who has placed himself on the other side of a line, which is a different picture from fighting across one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates knowing something from being governed by it, and treats the gap as the actual problem. That is a claim about how people go wrong: not usually through ignorance but through information held at a distance from action. Framing it as a question rather than an accusation also leaves the listener to close the gap themselves instead of being told they have failed.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for those who oppose God and His Messenger, describing where they rank.
Asks whether people who teach righteousness forget themselves while reciting the Book.
Compares those given knowledge who do not carry it to a donkey loaded with books.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you know perfectly well and act against anyway. Do not resolve to change it. Just write the sentence out: I know this, and I do that. Reading the two clauses next to each other in your own handwriting does something that deciding to do better does not.

studies.title: Afraid Of A Surah
studies.meaning: The fear described is very specific: that a surah might be sent down informing them of what is in their hearts. Not exposing what they did, which was already visible, but reporting the interior. The reply neither reassures nor denies. It says go on mocking, God will bring out the very thing you are afraid of. The fear and the answer are built from the same word.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, within the long section describing those who stayed behind. The commentators report that this part of the surah acquired a name among the early community reflecting exactly this, a surah that exposed. The passage is unusual in describing its own effect while producing it, which is why the commentaries treat these ayat as self-referential.

keyTerms.note: A verb for caution rather than terror, naming the alertness of someone expecting trouble. It appears twice in this ayah, once of them and once inside the reply, which turns their own word back on them.
The verb for conveying news of consequence. Its object here is themselves: the surah they fear would tell them what is in their own hearts, which is a strange and specific thing to dread.
An active participle from the verb to bring out. The reply uses a form describing something already under way rather than a future threat, so the bringing out is presented as in progress.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Revelation arrived in public and unpredictably. A passage could come down naming a situation everyone in the town recognised, and it would then be recited aloud, memorised, and repeated in the prayer for the rest of time. For anyone with something to conceal that was a different kind of exposure from gossip, because gossip fades and this did not.
studies.didYouKnow: The early tradition preserves more than one name for this surah, and one of them, reported from among the earliest commentators, means the exposer, given precisely because of passages like this one. A surah that describes people fearing a surah about themselves ended up named for that very effect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a fear of being known rather than of being punished, and it treats that fear as itself revealing. Someone worried about a report of their interior has already conceded that there is something in it. The reply then declines to argue, which is characteristic: it does not prove the charge, it says the matter will come out, and leaves the timing unstated.

crossReferences.why: Says those with sickness in their hearts assumed God would not bring out their rancour.
Describes people concealing in themselves what they would not disclose to the Prophet.
States that some near them were not known to them, but were known to God.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you would least want written down about your motives this week. Not your actions, your motives. You do not have to tell anyone at all. But the discomfort of naming it privately is exactly what this ayah describes, and it is easier to sit with once than to keep at bay indefinitely.

studies.title: We Were Only Talking
studies.meaning: The excuse is quoted exactly: we were only talking and playing. The reply does not dispute that they were joking. It asks what the joking was about, and names three objects: God, His signs, His Messenger. The second ayah then refuses the apology and, in the same breath, divides the group. If We pardon one party of you, We will punish another. The pardon is named as possible without being handed out.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the ayah about fearing exposure. The commentators connect the exchange to talk during the march north that was afterwards explained as jest. They note that the passage does not deny the jesting, and that the division named in the second ayah leaves both outcomes open without assigning any particular person to either.

keyTerms.note: A verb for wading into water, used of talk entered without care. It occurs here and at 74:45, once as a casual excuse and once among the reasons given by those in the fire.
The verb of offering an apology. It is refused rather than called false, which is a different act: the passage declines the transaction rather than disputing the account being given.

A conditional, with the pardon left unassigned. It stands in the same sentence as the punishment and neither is attached to anyone named, which commentators note as leaving the outcome genuinely open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Talk on a long march filled the hours, and men said things at the back of a column they would never have said standing still. Everyone knew the difference and everyone relied on it. The claim that something was only banter was the ordinary defence in that world, and it usually worked, because there was rarely anybody in a position to say otherwise.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the speakers use for their idle talk appears again at 74:45, where it turns up among the reasons the people of the fire give for being there. The same verb, of speech waded into without care, serves in one place as a casual excuse and in the other as an explanation offered far too late.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses an apology and offers a pardon in consecutive sentences, which looks contradictory until the difference is noticed. An apology would have settled the matter on the speaker's terms; a pardon leaves it with God. That distinction is the whole point. Forgiveness here is not withheld, it is simply not something a wrongdoer can produce by explaining himself.

crossReferences.why: Describes the fear of exposure that this exchange follows on from immediately.
Uses the same verb for idle talk, listed there among reasons given by those in the fire.
Tells a group not to make excuses, using the same refusal of an apology.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you said you were only joking. Ask what the joke was about, in one plain sentence, without the framing around it. The reply here does not argue about whether it was a joke. It asks for the object, which is usually the part that was doing the actual work.

studies.title: They Close Their Hands
studies.meaning: A group is described as being of one another, and then four things are named. They call for what is wrong, warn against what is right, and hold their hands closed. Then a sentence with a symmetry inside it: they forgot God, so He forgot them. The closed hand sits in the same list as the moral inversion, which is how the passage links a habit with money to a habit with truth.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, describing the group the surah has followed since the section on the march north. The commentators read the closing clause as a matching of form rather than a statement that God forgets, explaining it as God treating them as one treats what is forgotten. That reading is standard across the classical commentaries on the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A physical image of a fist closing. Arabic used the open and the closed hand as the standard picture of giving and withholding, so the phrase names stinginess without any abstract word for it.
The same construction appears four ayat later of believers, where it describes their being allies of one another. One phrase covers two groups, so the parallel between the passages is deliberate.
Commentators read the second verb as matching the first in form rather than in sense, since forgetting is not attributed to God. The phrase occurs only once in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The closed hand needed no explaining. Wealth moved by hand in that society: coins counted out, dates measured into a cloth, an animal led over and handed across. Generosity and its opposite were both physical acts performed in front of other people, which is why a description of a fist carried the entire meaning without a word of commentary.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and 9:71 are built as mirrors of each other. Both open with the same phrase about a group being part of one another, both list what the group calls for and warns against, and the two lists are exactly reversed. A few lines apart, the surah supplies its own contrast without remarking on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts moral inversion and withheld generosity in a single list, which suggests they are one disposition seen from two sides. It then describes the consequence as a matching: what was done is what is met. That form of consequence recurs throughout the Quran, and it keeps a punishment from looking arbitrary, since the outcome is shaped by the act rather than added onto it.

crossReferences.why: Mirrors this ayah exactly, listing the reverse for believing men and women.
Describes those who forgot God, and says He made them forget their own selves.
Uses the image of a hand held closed and a hand stretched out entirely.

studies.applyIt: Watch your hands this week, literally. Notice the moment you decide not to give something small: a tip, a lift, ten minutes of help. You are not obliged to change the decision. Just catch the physical instant of closing, which is what this ayah names, and see how fast the reason arrives afterwards.

studies.title: It Is Enough For Them
studies.meaning: The outcome is stated with the verb of promising, which Arabic ordinarily keeps for something good. Then a short clause: it is enough for them. The word for enough is the one used nine ayat earlier in the sentence about God being sufficient. The passage closes on a punishment described as resident rather than arriving, using the adjective the surah applied to the bliss of the gardens.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the description of the group in the previous ayah. The commentators read this ayah as the counterpart of 9:72, which uses the same verb of promising for believers four ayat later. The pairing runs through this whole section, where each description of one group is answered by its opposite within a few lines of text.

keyTerms.note: The verb of promising, which Arabic normally reserves for something hoped for. The Quran uses it here of a punishment, a usage commentators note as making the outcome certain rather than merely threatened.
The same word used at 9:59 in the sentence about God being sufficient. Placing it here creates a bleak symmetry, since what a person settles for is described as what suffices them.
The second word means residing or staying put, the same term used at 9:21 of the bliss in the gardens. One adjective covers both outcomes, differing only in what it is attached to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise in that society was a public instrument. Men made them before witnesses and were held to them for years, and the whole vocabulary of obligation ran through the word. Using it for something feared rather than hoped for would have registered at once, because it moved the outcome out of the category of a threat, which can be avoided, into that of a commitment.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a lasting punishment here uses the same adjective the surah applies at 9:21 to the bliss of the gardens, and the verb of promising reappears at 9:72 for the believers. Within a few dozen ayat the surah builds both destinations from one vocabulary, changing only what it attaches to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage uses the language of promise rather than of threat, and that changes its character. A threat invites calculation about whether it will actually be carried out; a promise does not. The symmetry with the corresponding ayat about believers also means neither description can be read alone, since the surah has deliberately made them from the same words.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of promising for believing men and women, four ayat later.
Applies the same adjective for lasting to the bliss of the gardens instead.
Describes the same group's position and the absence of any helper for them.

studies.applyIt: Notice the phrase it is enough for them. Ask what you have quietly settled for and called sufficient: a level of attention, a quality of relationship, a way of spending an evening. Naming one honestly this week is uncomfortable and useful, because sufficiency is a decision people make without ever noticing.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: You Enjoyed Your Portion
studies.meaning: The comparison is made and then made again, and the repetition is the argument. Those before you were stronger, richer, with more children. They enjoyed their portion, and you have enjoyed your portion as those before you enjoyed theirs, and you waded in as they waded. The same two words return three times each. Then the verdict: their works came to nothing in both worlds.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, addressing the group described through this section. The commentators read the ayah as placing its audience inside a sequence rather than singling them out, and they note the shift midway from speaking about those before to addressing the listener directly. Appealing to the pattern of earlier communities is the surah's usual way of widening a local situation.

keyTerms.note: A word for an allotted share of this world's goods. The ayah uses it three times in one sentence, naming the same allotment for each generation in turn without any of them receiving more.

keyTerms.gloss: so they enjoyed, took their use
keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to take one's use out of something. The word is not a criticism in itself, since the Quran uses it of legitimate enjoyment, and the fault named is where it stopped.
The same verb used four ayat earlier by the men who said they had only been talking. Its reappearance here places their excuse inside a much older and larger pattern.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruins were visible. Trade routes north and south passed abandoned settlements, rock-cut tombs and dead wells belonging to peoples whose names survived in poetry and nowhere else. Caravans camped beside them. An audience told that earlier communities had been stronger and richer was not being asked to imagine anything; they had walked past the evidence.
studies.didYouKnow: One word for an allotted share appears three times inside this single ayah, and the verb for taking enjoyment appears three times alongside it. The Quran rarely repeats vocabulary at that density, and here the repetition performs the point, since each generation is described in exactly the words used for the last.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies its audience the assumption of being a special case. By describing them in precisely the words used for earlier peoples, it makes a local situation an instance rather than an event. That is deflating and also clarifying: what happened before is what is happening, and the outcome named for them is available on the same terms.

crossReferences.why: Names the specific earlier communities this ayah has been referring to in general terms.
Warns against being impressed by the movement of those who disbelieve through the land.
Points to earlier peoples who were stronger and cultivated the earth more than these.

studies.applyIt: Take the situation you feel is uniquely yours and find one person, from another decade or another country, who has been in it. Read about them for ten minutes. The method here is to remove the sense of being a special case, and it usually turns out to be a relief rather than a diminishment.

studies.title: Six Peoples In One Line
studies.meaning: A question is asked and answered by a list. Has the account of those before them not reached them: the people of Noah, Aad, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Midian, and the overturned cities. Six entries, then a single clause covering all of them, that their messengers came with clear signs. The passage ends by placing the fault precisely, on them rather than on God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators identify the peoples named as a sequence the Quran uses repeatedly, some Arabian and some further afield, and note that the last entry refers to the settlements associated with Lot. The list is offered to an audience for whom several of these places lay on known trade routes rather than in a distant and unvisited past.

keyTerms.note: A word for weighty news rather than a story. The Quran uses it of reports carrying an implication for the hearer, which is why the sentence asks whether it reached them rather than whether they enjoyed it.
A participle meaning turned upside down. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 69:9, and the commentators identify it with the settlements associated with Lot.
From a root meaning to be distinct or evident. The word covers proofs and wonders alike, and its use here says the failure was never one of insufficient evidence being supplied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Two of the peoples named left ruins on routes that Meccan traders used. Rock-cut facades in the north stood beside the road to Syria, and stories about who had carved them were common currency at the fairs. When this list was recited, part of it referred to places in the audience's own working geography rather than to legend.
studies.didYouKnow: Six peoples are named in one sentence here and then covered by a single clause: their messengers came to them with clear signs. The Quran usually gives each of these accounts a whole passage of its own, and this ayah compresses all of them into one line, among the tightest forms the sequence ever takes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the fault carefully. It does not say these peoples were destroyed for their opinions; it says messengers came with clear signs and that God did not wrong them. Putting the wrong on their own account keeps the sequence from becoming a story about divine temper, and it implies that the pattern concerns response rather than identity.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same comparison in general terms, which this ayah fills in with names.
Lists an overlapping sequence of communities that rejected the messengers sent to them.
Names the overturned city, using the singular of the word that appears here.

studies.applyIt: Read one of the accounts this list compresses, in full, this week: the people of Noah, or of Midian. Ten minutes with a whole story rather than a name inside a list. The ayah assumes its audience already knows them, and that assumption is worth earning rather than passing over.

studies.title: Allies Of One Another
studies.meaning: The word used is not friendship but alliance, the term for people bound to protect and answer for one another. Men and women are named in the same clause and given the same standing in it. Five activities follow, and the first two are public: enjoining what is good and forbidding what is wrong, duties that belonged to people with standing rather than to dependants. The promise at the end carries a future marker, mercy still to come.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah. The ayah stands opposite an earlier description of the disaffected, who are said to be of one another in a matching construction, so the two groups are defined by the same grammar and distinguished by what they do together. The commentators point to that pairing, and read this ayah as the positive half of a deliberate contrast.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for the person who stands closest and takes responsibility, used of a guardian and of a patron. It names a relationship carrying obligations rather than an affection.
A verb of command rather than of suggestion. Giving it to the whole community, women included, distributes an authority that in that society belonged to heads of households and clan leaders.
The verb carries a prefix marking future time, which the commentators notice. Mercy is promised as coming rather than as already held, so the list preceding it is not presented as a receipt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliance in Arabia was a formal act. Two parties or two clans swore mutual protection, and the bond obliged each to defend the other and to pay for their wrongs. It could be entered into by people with no blood relation, and in practice it outranked many family ties. Describing believing men and women as allies used the strongest available word for a bond that was chosen.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names believing men and believing women with separate words in a single clause, and the surah does the same for the disaffected a few ayat earlier. The pairing is not a stylistic habit; the Quran uses it where a claim about standing is being made, and the longest example runs ten such pairs in one ayah of surah 33.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Religious community is defined by mutual obligation rather than by shared belief alone, and the obligations named are public ones. Placing the duty to enjoin and forbid at the head of the list gives every member a share in the community's direction, which is a claim about who counts as responsible. The closing promise then keeps that from becoming self-congratulation by putting mercy in the future.

crossReferences.why: Describes the opposite group in a matching construction, defined by what they do together.
Extends the same pairing of men and women through ten qualities in one ayah.
Assigns the same public duty of calling to good to a group within the community.

studies.applyIt: Name one person in your community whose difficulty you know about and have been treating as their business rather than yours. Do one concrete thing about it this week, even a small one. The word this ayah uses is not friendship. It describes people who have accepted a claim on each other, and claims are met in specifics.

studies.title: Greater Than The Gardens
studies.meaning: A promise is made at length and then something is declared greater than it. Gardens with rivers running beneath, good dwellings, gardens of lasting residence, and then four words: acceptance from God is greater. The next ayah gives an instruction of an entirely different temperature. The two stand side by side and the surah does not soften the join between them at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators pair this promise with the corresponding warning at 9:68, which uses the same verb of promising four ayat earlier. The instruction that follows belongs to the section on the march north and its aftermath. This part of the surah routinely places its warmest and its hardest material adjacent, which the commentaries note as a feature of it.

keyTerms.note: The first word names a place of rest and settling, from the same root as the calm sent down at 9:26. The promise therefore includes somewhere to live rather than only a landscape to be in.
The second word names permanence of dwelling, and the same root gives the Arabic word for a mine, something fixed in place. The phrase occurs eleven times across the Quran.
The clause is short and stands alone after a long description. It ranks a relation above a place without withdrawing the place, which is why the description comes first and is not shortened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dwelling that stayed was the rarer half of the promise. Many people in that world moved with water and pasture, striking a camp and rebuilding it somewhere else several times a year. Permanent housing belonged to the settled towns and to the wealthier families in them. A garden and a house that never had to be left were two promises, not one.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause saying that acceptance from God is greater is four words long in Arabic and follows a description of the gardens several lines long. The surah had already implied the ordering at 9:21, where the same three elements appear in the same sequence, and here it states the comparison outright.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a relation above a place, and then the following ayah moves straight into an instruction that shares none of its warmth. Read together they deny the reader any settled emotional register. That is characteristic of this surah, which keeps promise and demand in contact rather than separating them into different parts of the text.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same three elements in the same order, without stating the comparison outright.
Ends on God being pleased with them and they with Him, in the same order.
Uses the same verb of promising four ayat earlier, of the opposite outcome.

studies.applyIt: Read the four-word clause on its own: acceptance from God is greater. Then notice that the surah moves immediately into something hard. Try holding both in one sitting this week rather than picking a mood. Most people read scripture for one register at a time, and this passage is arranged to prevent that.

studies.title: Resentful For Being Enriched
studies.meaning: The longest ayah in this section moves through five stages. They swear they said nothing; they did say it; they rejected after their submission; they aimed at something they did not reach. Then a diagnosis that is not what anyone expects: their resentment came from nothing except having been enriched. And after all of that, a door is opened. If they repent it would be better for them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, after the return from the march north. The commentators connect the ayah to an incident reported during that journey and preserve more than one account of what was said and by whom. They agree on the structure: a list of charges followed by an offer, with the offer placed before the alternative rather than after it.

keyTerms.gloss: they aimed and did not reach
keyTerms.note: The verb names an intention formed and acted on, and the clause says only that it failed. Nothing at all is described, which the commentators treat as deliberate reticence about the incident.
A verb for finding fault and taking revenge for a wrong. Its object here is a benefit, so the sentence says the grievance was produced by the very thing that helped them.

keyTerms.gloss: He enriched them, made them independent
keyTerms.note: From the root for sufficiency and wealth. Commentators note that the enrichment is attributed to God and the Messenger together, and that the resentment is dated from it rather than from any injury.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sudden prosperity was socially awkward in a society of fixed ranks. A man raised by an unexpected share, or by a change in a city's fortunes, owed his new position to whoever had arranged it, and the debt was visible to everyone. Resentment of a benefactor was common enough that poets wrote about it, and this ayah names the pattern without softening it.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah lists four charges and then, before naming any consequence, offers repentance. That ordering recurs through this surah: at 9:3, at 9:5 and at 9:11 the door is stated before or alongside the alternative rather than after it, so the sequence belongs to the surah rather than to this passage alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a specific and unattractive mechanism: being helped can produce resentment rather than gratitude, because a benefit places a person in someone's debt. Naming that as the entire cause of a grievance is a hard observation about people. And then the ayah offers the same exit it offers everyone else, so the mechanism disqualifies nobody from using it.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with another case of bounty received and a promise left unkept.
Refuses an apology while leaving a pardon open, in the same section and the same pattern.
Describes whose repentance is accepted and the conditions under which it is received.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose help you have never quite forgiven. Not an enemy, a benefactor. Most people have one, and the discomfort is real rather than shameful. Name what the help cost you in standing, then decide separately whether the resentment is worth keeping. Separating those two questions is most of the work.

studies.title: The Promise Made In Need
studies.meaning: A vow is quoted in full: if He gives us of His bounty, we will certainly give in charity and be among the upright. Both verbs carry the strongest emphatic form Arabic has. Then the next sentence is short and flat. When He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it and turned away. The grammar of the promise and the grammar of the failure could not be further apart.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the ayat about contributions withheld during preparations for the march north. The commentators preserve an account of a particular man who made such a vow, with variations in the details. They read the passage as describing a pattern rather than one incident, since the ayat around it concern giving in general.

keyTerms.gloss: we will certainly give in charity
keyTerms.note: The verb carries both an emphatic prefix and an emphatic ending, the strongest oath form available. It occurs only once in the Quran, so the most heavily reinforced pledge in this vocabulary is one that was broken.
The identical phrase appears in both ayat, once in the request and once in the giving. Nothing at all changed between them except what the recipients then did, which is what the repetition isolates.
The verb for withholding what one has. It arrives with no explanation attached to it, and that flatness is part of the effect after the elaborate promise in the ayah before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Vows conditional on relief were ordinary religious practice across Arabia. A man in difficulty pledged an animal, a share of a harvest, or a journey, and the pledge bound him publicly if the relief arrived. Everyone had heard such vows made, and had watched some of them honoured and others quietly dropped once the danger had passed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb in the vow, that they would certainly give in charity, occurs only once in the Quran and carries both of the emphatic markers Arabic can attach to a promise. The most reinforced pledge in the whole text is the one the very next ayah reports being broken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the intensity of a promise against what followed it and lets the contrast do the work. It suggests that the force of a resolution says nothing about the outcome, because the conditions that produce fervent promises are exactly the ones that pass. That is a claim about timing rather than sincerity, and it makes gratitude a question of what happens after relief.

crossReferences.why: States the consequence attached to this broken promise in the ayah that immediately follows.
Describes people at sea who promise gratitude and forget it once they reach land.
Uses the same pattern, calling on God in danger and turning away once saved.

studies.applyIt: Remember what you promised during the last thing you were desperate about. Not to feel bad about it. Just to find the sentence again and see whether any of it was kept. If none of it was, make a much smaller version of the same promise now, while nothing is wrong, and keep that one.

studies.title: A Burrow With Two Exits
studies.meaning: The consequence is described as something trailing behind an act rather than imposed on top of it. He left a doubleness following in their hearts until the day they meet Him, and the reason is given twice over: because they failed what they promised God, and because they were lying. The second ayah then asks whether they do not know that God knows their secret and their private talk.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the broken vow described in the previous ayat. The commentators note that the passage describes a consequence continuing over time rather than a punishment delivered once, and they attend to the sequence: the breaking of a promise comes first, and the condition of the heart follows from it rather than preceding it.

keyTerms.gloss: so He left it following them
keyTerms.note: From the root for a heel and for what comes afterwards. The verb describes a consequence trailing an act rather than being applied to it, so the condition arrives as a sequel to what was done.
The noun occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah. Its root describes a burrow with a second exit, which is the image beneath the word: a way out kept hidden at the back.
A word for talk conducted apart from others. Naming it beside the inner secret extends the sentence from what a person thinks to what they say in small rooms with a few people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The image inside the word came from the desert. Certain burrowing animals dig a tunnel with a concealed second opening, so that when a hunter breaks in at the front the animal is already leaving at the back. Anyone who had hunted or watched a hunt understood the picture, and the word carried it without needing any explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: The noun used here occurs only twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, at this ayah and again at 9:97. Its root describes a burrow with a hidden second exit, so the term names a structure rather than a feeling: a position held with an escape already dug behind it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the act before the condition. A promise was broken, and the state of the heart followed from that rather than causing it, which reverses the order people usually assume. That has a consequence for how a person reads themselves: what one does shapes what one becomes, and a disposition can be acquired through a series of small failures to keep something.

crossReferences.why: Records the promise whose breaking this ayah names as the cause of what follows.
Names a sickness in the heart that was increased, describing a condition that develops.
Says that what people used to earn has covered over their hearts like rust.

studies.applyIt: Notice one small promise you have broken more than once, to somebody who never mentions it. The order here is unsettling and useful: the act came first and the condition followed. Keep that particular promise this week, exactly, once. Not as a resolution. As a test of the sequence.

studies.title: Nothing But Their Own Effort
studies.meaning: Two groups are being mocked and the passage names both. Those who give voluntarily beyond what is asked, and those who find nothing to give except their own effort. The second is the crueller target, since what is being ridiculed there is smallness itself. The reply uses the mockers' own verb back at them. Nothing is argued; the sentence answers in the register they chose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, during the collection for the march north. The commentators report that contributions ranged from very large gifts to men who could offer only a day's wages carried in by hand, and that both ends were being ridiculed, the large as display and the small as pointless. The ayah names the two together for exactly that reason.

keyTerms.note: A form built on willing obedience, describing what is offered beyond anything due. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it names the giving that has no obligation behind it and therefore no defence.
The word covers capacity strained to its limit. Applied to a contribution it means the person gave everything available, so what was mocked as small was in fact complete.
The verb for derision. The reply uses the identical verb with God as its subject, so the sentence answers mockery with the same word rather than with an argument against it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Contributions were brought in and set down where people could see them. A man arriving with a large gift was noticed, and so was one arriving with a handful of dates earned by drawing water through the night. In a town that size both walked past the same crowd, and both were talked about afterwards, which is the situation being described.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who give voluntarily occurs only once in the whole Quran, here, and it is built on a root meaning willing compliance. The Quran therefore has a specific term for giving beyond what is due, and it appears at the moment such giving is being ridiculed rather than praised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage protects both ends of a range at once, which is unusual. It defends the large gift against the charge of display and the tiny gift against the charge of insignificance, in one sentence and without ranking them. That leaves no position from which a contribution can safely be mocked, and it makes the capacity of the giver the measure rather than the amount given.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same group finding fault about charity, earlier in the surah.
Discusses giving openly and giving in secret, and what each of them is good for.
Instructs people to be conscious of God as much as they are actually able.

studies.applyIt: Watch what you think when you see someone give conspicuously, and what you think when you see someone give a token amount. Both reactions arrive fast and neither is flattering. This ayah defends both givers in a single sentence, which leaves the observer nowhere to stand. Notice where you had been standing.

studies.title: Even Seventy Times
studies.meaning: A choice is offered and then dissolved. Ask forgiveness for them or do not; even if you ask seventy times, God will not forgive them. The number does rhetorical work rather than arithmetic, and the commentators discuss whether it names a limit or simply a large indefinite quantity. What the ayah addresses is not the mercy but the intercession: asking is not the mechanism, and the reason given is what they did.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the ayat about those who stayed behind. The commentators preserve a discussion about whether the number is exact and record more than one view. A closely parallel statement appears at 63:6, and the classical commentaries read the two together, noting that both passages close on the same clause about guidance.

keyTerms.note: Seventy serves in Arabic for a large indefinite number as well as for a count. Commentators record both readings, and the only other occurrence of the word in the Quran is at 7:155.
The verb of seeking pardon on behalf of somebody else. The imperative and its negation stand side by side in one clause, presenting the two options as equivalent before either is evaluated.
The negative particle denies a future emphatically. Commentators tie the denial to the description that follows rather than to the number, so the reason given is conduct and not any count.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession was how that world worked. A man in trouble found somebody with standing to speak for him, and the speaker's reputation, rather than the petitioner's case, often decided the outcome. That system ran through every court, market and tribal council in Arabia. An ayah saying intercession will not move the decision was addressing the most familiar mechanism its audience had.
studies.didYouKnow: The word seventy occurs only twice in the Quran. The other place is 7:155, where Moses chooses seventy men from his people for an appointed meeting. Outside these two passages the number never appears, which is part of why the commentators discuss whether it is meant here as a count at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes intercession as a mechanism without denying mercy. What it rules out is the transfer of a decision from the person who acted to somebody willing to speak for them. That returns responsibility to where the surah keeps placing it, and it also guards against a religion of connections, in which access to the right person substitutes for everything else.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing in almost identical words, closing on the same clause about guidance.
Continues the same subject later in the surah, about asking forgiveness for those who died rejecting.
States that nobody intercedes except by His permission, the general principle behind this.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you resolve a problem by finding somebody to speak for you rather than by dealing with it directly. The habit is efficient and mostly harmless. This ayah names one place where it does not reach, which is worth knowing before you have need of it rather than afterwards.

studies.title: Do Not Go Out In The Heat
studies.meaning: The scene is domestic and the reply is not. Those left behind were glad of their sitting, hated to strive with wealth and person, and said to one another: do not go out in the heat. Their sentence is quoted exactly, and it is entirely reasonable advice. The answer takes their own word and extends it: the fire is hotter. Then a clause, if only they understood.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The march north fell in the hottest part of the year, when crossing open ground in daylight was genuinely dangerous, and the commentators nowhere dispute that the advice quoted was sound as advice. The surah records the sentence as spoken and answers it on a different scale rather than contesting the fact it rests on.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle: those who were left rather than those who chose to stay. The form recurs through this section, and commentators note that it does not by itself say who did the leaving.

keyTerms.gloss: do not go out in heat
keyTerms.note: The verb is the same one used at 9:38 and 9:41 for moving out. Here it stands in a negative imperative spoken by people to each other rather than as an instruction given to them.
A comparative built directly on the word they had used. The phrase occurs only once in the Quran, and the reply works by extending their own term rather than by introducing a new one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Summer travel in that region killed people. Ground temperatures made midday movement impossible, water sources lay far apart and were sometimes dry, and animals failed before men did. Caravans routinely waited the season out. The sentence quoted here was the standard, sensible counsel of everyone who had crossed that country, which is exactly what makes it hard to answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative phrase in the reply occurs only once in the Quran, and it is built out of the very word the speakers used. The answer introduces no new vocabulary; it takes the term of the excuse and sets it on a different scale, which is a pattern this section of the surah uses more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not deny the fact the excuse rests on. The heat was real. What it disputes is the scale on which the calculation was made, which is a different kind of correction from calling something false. It leaves the reasoning intact and changes only its frame, implying that most self-deception is a matter of scope rather than of accuracy.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for moving out, describing this reluctance from the outside.
Answers another excuse by taking hold of the very word its speaker chose.
States the general principle that human assessment of good and harm is limited.

studies.applyIt: Take a reason you have given for not doing something, and check whether it is factually true. It probably is. Then ask what scale you were weighing it on, and whether a longer one exists. The correction here is not that the excuse was false. It is that the frame was small.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Laugh A Little, Weep Much
studies.meaning: Two imperatives, eight words in Arabic, and the whole sentence turns on two adverbs. Let them laugh a little and weep much, in recompense for what they were earning. Nothing is described, no scene is set, and no timeframe is attached to either half. The contrast is between quantities of time, and the reader is left to supply which portion belongs where.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the sentence about the heat. The commentators read the two imperatives as descriptive rather than as orders, a construction Arabic uses to state what will be the case. They place the ayah among the shortest in the surah, set between two much longer passages about the same group and the same expedition.

keyTerms.note: An imperative used to state an outcome rather than to issue an order, a construction Arabic has and English lacks. The commentators read both verbs in this ayah in that way.
The verb for weeping occurs in this form only once in the Quran. Set directly against laughing in the same sentence, it makes the ayah a comparison of two durations rather than of two moods.
The verb for acquiring by work, used throughout the Quran of deeds. It makes the outcome something accumulated rather than assigned, which is why the sentence calls it a recompense.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weeping was not private in that culture. Grief was performed at funerals by whole households and sometimes by hired women, and it was heard across a settlement. Laughter carried in the same way. Both were audible community events rather than interior states, so a sentence measuring one against the other described something the audience could picture as sound.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the shortest ayat in the surah, eight words in Arabic, and it sits between two of the longest passages about the same group. The verb for weeping appears in this form only here in the Quran, so the briefest sentence in the section also contains one of its rarest words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures in time rather than in intensity. A little and much are quantities, and setting them against each other says the error was one of proportion: something brief was preferred to something long. That framing avoids any claim about how bad the laughing was, and it turns the judgement into arithmetic the listener can do without help.

crossReferences.why: States that it is God who makes people laugh and weep, using the same two verbs.
Supplies the situation, the pleasure taken in sitting out, that this ayah answers.
Describes preferring this life to the next as a choice between the short and the lasting.

studies.applyIt: Take something you are enjoying that you know is costing you later: an hour, a habit, an avoidance. Do not stop it today. Just put a number on both sides, the minutes gained and the time spent afterwards, and look at the two numbers together. That is the whole operation this ayah performs.

studies.title: Content To Sit The First Time
studies.meaning: A future situation is imagined and a reply is prepared for it in advance. If God returns you to a group of them and they ask leave to come out, say: you will never come out with me, nor fight an enemy alongside me. Then the reason, and it is their own word turned around. You were content to sit the first time, so sit with those who stay. A choice is allowed to stand.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, given before or during the return from the march north. The commentators note that the ayah anticipates a request that had not yet been made. It belongs to a run of passages about the same group, and the reply it supplies uses the vocabulary of contentment that the surah applies elsewhere to shares and to God.

keyTerms.note: The verb of being satisfied, the same root used at 9:59 for contentment with what God gives. Here it names contentment fixed on the wrong object, so one word covers both the virtue and its misdirection.
A participle from the root for coming after or being left. This form occurs only once in the Quran, though a related form appears twice more in this same surah, at 9:87 and 9:93.
The emphatic negative is reinforced by a word meaning ever. The severity lies in the permanence, and the commentators discuss whether it applies to that campaign or reaches beyond it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being excluded from an expedition was a lasting mark. Campaigns were where reputations were made, shares distributed and alliances formed, so a man barred from the next one was barred from all of that, and his sons would hear about it. The reply prepared here is not a rebuke but a social consequence, and its weight was obvious to everyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who stay behind in this ayah occurs only once in the Quran, and two related forms from the same root appear at 9:87 and 9:93, both also in this surah. The whole family of words belongs to this one section, which is describing a single situation in detail.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a choice become a condition. Nothing new is imposed; the reply simply confirms what was chosen the first time and declines to reopen it. That is a serious account of how decisions work, since it treats a preference exercised once as having settled something. It also applies the word for contentment, used elsewhere of God, to a settling in the wrong place.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of contentment, there of being satisfied with what God gives.
Uses a related word for those left at home, describing the same group again.
Anticipates a similar request to come along once there is something to be gained.

studies.applyIt: Notice a door you closed by declining once, without meaning it as a permanent answer. Some of them stay closed, and the closing is not unfair. If you want one of them open again, the work is not a request but a different first answer next time it comes around, which is usually sooner than expected.

studies.title: The Rite The Community Withholds
studies.meaning: Two things are named, and both are done for the dead rather than to them. Do not pray over any of them who dies, and do not stand at his grave. What is described concerns the community's rites rather than the person's standing, which is settled in the clause that follows. Withheld here is the last public act by which a group claims someone as one of its own.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, among the passages about those who stayed behind. The commentators read the instruction as addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about specific individuals whose position had already become clear, and they discuss its relation to a reported occasion. The ayat surrounding it concern the same group and the same expedition.

keyTerms.note: The verb of prayer with a preposition that makes it prayer on someone's behalf. The construction names the funeral rite specifically rather than prayer in general, which is why a second clause adds the grave.

keyTerms.gloss: do not stand at his grave
keyTerms.note: Standing at a grave was a distinct act from the prayer, performed after burial. Naming both closes the two public occasions on which a community marks that somebody was theirs.
The word for ever attaches to the instruction rather than to the dying. Its placement makes the matter permanent, matching the same term used one ayah earlier about never going out together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A funeral was the moment a community confirmed who belonged to it. The prayer was performed in ranks by whoever could attend, the body was carried by neighbours, and standing at the grave afterwards was a public act of association. To withhold all of that was not a comment on the dead person's fate; it was the community declining to make its usual claim.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for ever appears in this ayah and again in the one immediately before it, attached both times to a refusal. Two consecutive ayat close the same door, one for the living and one for the dead, using the identical term for permanence in each case.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes a community's rites from a person's standing with God. What is instructed concerns what the community does, and the clause giving the reason concerns what the individuals had done, but nothing here claims the rite would have altered anything. That separation matters, because it keeps a public act from being mistaken for a transaction with God.

crossReferences.why: Makes the parallel point about asking forgiveness, that it is not the mechanism.
Uses the same word for permanence one ayah earlier, refusing a different request.
Describes the same refusal of intercession for a group in another Medinan surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your religious life is public marking rather than private address: attendance, presence, being seen at the right occasions. None of it is worthless. But this ayah separates the two sharply, and it is worth checking privately which of them you would miss more if it were taken away.

studies.title: The Same Sentence, A New Place
studies.meaning: This ayah repeats almost exactly what was said at 9:55, and its position has changed what it does. There it followed a description of contributions given unwillingly. Here it follows an instruction about funerals and graves. The same words about wealth and children now stand beside a death, so the objects being admired sit immediately next to the moment they stop being any use.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, thirty ayat after its first occurrence and in a very different setting. The commentators note the repetition and read it as emphasis rather than oversight, observing that this section of the surah restates several of its earlier statements in sharper contexts. The ayah before concerns burial and the one after returns to exemptions.

keyTerms.gloss: and let it not impress you
keyTerms.note: The opening differs by a single particle from the version at 9:55, and the reciters preserve both exactly. Everything else in the two ayat is nearly identical, so the variation is small and deliberate.
Shorter here than at 9:55, which says in the life of this world. The compression fits the position, since the ayah now stands beside a grave and needs no further reminder of which world is meant.
The word covers the self and the soul at once, so a departure of the soul is also a departure of the person. Placed after the funeral instruction, it names from the inside what was just described.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A funeral was where a man's estate first became visible as a set of objects. The animals, the stored grain, the house, and the sons who would inherit were all present in one place on one afternoon. Anyone who had stood at a graveside in that world had seen wealth and children assembled beside a body, which is exactly the arrangement of these two ayat.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and 9:55 are the only substantial repetition in the surah, differing by a handful of particles across a single sentence. The commentators note that the second occurrence is slightly the shorter of the two, and that its position directly after the passage on funerals is what the repetition is for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes its force from placement rather than from content, since the content had already been given. Reading the same sentence in a new position changes what it does, which is a claim about how a text works on somebody over time. It sets possession beside death without comment, and leaves the reader to make the connection the arrangement offers.

crossReferences.why: Contains this same ayah almost word for word, in a different setting much earlier.
Precedes it with an instruction about funerals, which gives this repetition its position.
Describes rivalry in accumulation continuing right up until people visit the graves.

studies.applyIt: Read this ayah, then read 9:55, then read the ayah just before this one. Five minutes. Notice that the same sentence lands differently after a passage about a grave. That effect is not a trick of the text; it is what any sentence does when its neighbours change, including sentences you say to yourself.

studies.title: The Men Of Means Ask Leave
studies.meaning: A surah comes down saying believe in God and strive alongside His Messenger, and the men of means among them ask to be excused. Their sentence is quoted: leave us, we will be with those who sit. The second ayah then names what they chose and what followed from it. They were content to be among those left at home, and their hearts were sealed, so they do not understand.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators note that the people described are identified by wealth rather than by anything else, and that they were the ones best placed to equip themselves for the march north. The sealing described in the second ayah is discussed across the classical commentaries as following a settled pattern of refusal rather than preceding any choice.

keyTerms.note: The second word names abundance and reach. It occurs twice in the Quran, and the other occurrence at 40:3 uses it of God as the one of bounty, so a single term names both the source and these recipients.
A plural from the root for remaining behind. It occurs twice, both times in this surah, and the commentators note that it usually described those who stayed when a household travelled.
The verb for stamping a seal into clay or wax. The passive leaves the agent unstated, and the classical commentaries discuss the sealing as following repeated refusal rather than causing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth was what made participation possible. A man of means could equip himself and others, provide mounts, and carry provisions for a long route, so his absence subtracted more than one person from a column. Everyone doing the arithmetic in Medina that summer knew which households could have made the difference and which genuinely could not.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing these men as people of means occurs twice in the Quran. The other place is 40:3, where the same term is used of God as the possessor of abundance. One word therefore names the source of all bounty in one passage and, in this one, the men who declined to part with any of theirs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage links understanding to willingness rather than to capacity. The sealing is stated after the preference and not before it, so it reads as a habit settling rather than an obstacle placed in the way. That makes comprehension something a person can lose by repeated choice, which is a more uncomfortable account of guidance than one where it is simply given or withheld.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for those left at home, later in the same section of the surah.
Describes a sealing of hearts and hearing, using the same passive construction.
Uses the same word for abundance, there as a description of God Himself.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you have stopped understanding because you long ago stopped trying to: a subject, a person's point of view, a practice you dropped. The order in this ayah is preference first, then not understanding. Spend twenty minutes this week reopening one of them, and see whether the understanding follows the willingness.

studies.title: For Them Are The Good Things
studies.meaning: The passage turns on a single word: but. The Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their persons, and for them are the good things, and they are the ones who prosper. Then a garden is described. What stands out is the phrase for the good things, plural and unspecified, which arrives before the garden rather than as a summary of it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the description of those who asked to be excused. The commentators read the two passages as a deliberate pair, the second beginning with the contrastive particle that ties it to the first. Setting a description beside its opposite runs through this whole section of the surah.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the word for good, left unspecified. Commentators read it as covering benefits in this world and the next, and note that it is stated before the garden rather than as a description of it.
From a root meaning to split open, used of a farmer breaking soil. The Quran's word for success comes from cultivation, so prospering carries the sense of work that opens something up.
The verb of making ready in advance, from the same root as the preparation found missing at 9:46. Those who made no preparation are answered by a preparation already made for others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Splitting the ground was where everything began in a farming settlement. Medina lived on date palms and irrigated plots, and the first act of a season was breaking the soil so that water and seed could enter. The word this ayah uses for success came from that act, and the audience heard the farming inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for success used here comes from a root meaning to split open, the verb used of a farmer breaking the ground. The same root gives the Arabic word for a ploughman, so the Quran's vocabulary for prospering is agricultural rather than commercial, and it names labour rather than arrival.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the good things before it names the garden, which places something in this life inside the promise rather than deferring all of it. It also builds its word for success out of labour that opens the ground, so prospering is described as what happens when effort breaks something rather than as a destination reached. That is a working image, not a resting one.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who asked to be excused, the contrast this passage is set against.
Distinguishes the same two groups by a degree, using the same pairing of wealth and person.
Opens by naming the believers as those who prosper, using the same word.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the good things come before the garden in this sentence. Ask what a good thing in your ordinary week would be, and whether you would recognise it as part of a promise rather than as ordinary luck. Name one from the last seven days. The naming is the whole exercise.

studies.title: Those Who Came And Those Who Sat
