studies.meaning: Two groups are distinguished by what they did rather than by what they said. Some came presenting excuses and asking to be let off. Others, who had been untrue to God and His Messenger, simply stayed where they were and asked for nothing at all. The ayah records both, and the second is named more harshly. The word for those who came carries an ambiguity the reciters have preserved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, after the march north. The ayah opens a passage about the desert tribes around Medina, who appear more often in this surah than anywhere else in the Quran. The commentators note a long-standing difference over the word describing those who came: read one way it means offering an excuse, read another it means having a real one.

keyTerms.note: The word occurs only once in the Quran and carries two readings, one meaning those who invent an excuse and the other those who genuinely have one. Both are preserved in the recitation tradition.
The word names people living outside the settled towns, and it occurs ten times in the Quran, six of them in this surah. It describes a way of life rather than an ancestry.

keyTerms.gloss: and they sat, they stayed put
keyTerms.note: The plain verb for sitting down. Set against those who came and asked, it describes people who did not go through even the motion of a request, which is the contrast being drawn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribes outside the town had a different relationship with it. They came in for markets and for arbitration, and they were drawn into expeditions by agreement rather than by residence. Some sent men, some sent excuses, some heard nothing and did nothing. Distance made all three easy, and it made the difference between them hard to see from Medina.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who came with excuses occurs only once in the Quran, and it is one of the places where the recitation tradition preserves two readings with genuinely different senses, one describing men who invented a reason and the other men who had one. Both are transmitted rather than one being chosen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records the ambiguity rather than resolving it, and the tradition has kept the ambiguity for centuries. That says something about how the text expects to be read: two groups arrive inside one word, and the reader is handed no rule for telling them apart. What follows in the surah then treats each case separately and at length.

crossReferences.why: Names the people who genuinely carry no obligation, immediately after this ayah.
Names the group who do carry blame, those who ask while being wealthy.
Records excuses offered by the same desert tribes after a different expedition.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between someone who explains and someone who simply does not turn up. The first is easier to be irritated by and usually the better sign. Give one person this week the benefit of that distinction, especially if their explanation was clumsy or arrived too late to be any use.

studies.title: No Way Against Those Who Do Good
studies.meaning: Three groups are named and released: the weak, the sick, and those who find nothing to spend. One condition attaches, that they are sincere toward God and His Messenger, and nothing further is asked of them. A general clause then covers them all, that there is no way against those who do good. The sentence closes on two names of God, which turns an exemption into something warmer than a permission.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, after the march north. The commentators note that this ayah and the next define the boundary the surah has been circling: who is genuinely excused. The list is given in terms of capacity rather than of status, so it reaches people at every social level, and the surah turns immediately afterwards to those who had capacity and asked anyway.

keyTerms.note: The word originally names a narrow place with no room to move. Used of obligation it means the pressure of being held to something, so removing it is described as opening a space rather than granting leave.

The verb covers giving honest counsel and being genuinely committed. The single condition attached to this exemption concerns the interior, since nothing external could be asked of people who have nothing.

keyTerms.gloss: those who do good, do well
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning beauty as well as goodness, describing work done well rather than merely correctly. Applying it to people who did nothing at all is this ayah's most generous move.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Exemption in a tribal expedition was informal and therefore contested. A man with a limp, an old wound, or an empty store had to make his case to his own people, and the judgement was social. Naming three categories openly took the question out of the hands of neighbours who might otherwise have decided it by reputation.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for blame originally names a narrow place, somewhere too tight to move in. The Quran uses the same word at 22:78 to say that no such narrowness has been placed on people in religion, so one term links an individual exemption to a general statement about obligation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the standard at capacity rather than at output, and then calls the people who produced nothing doers of good. That is a substantial claim: the quality of a life is not measured by what it managed. The closing names of God are the same pair used elsewhere after far graver matters, which places an exemption inside mercy rather than beside it.

crossReferences.why: States that no narrowness has been placed on people in religion, using the same word.
States that God does not burden any soul beyond what it can bear.
Continues with those who wept because they could find nothing to give.

studies.applyIt: Think of what you are unable to do at present and have been quietly counting as a failure: an illness, a shortage, a stretch with nothing left over. Read the closing clause of this ayah as being about you. It calls people in exactly that position doers of good, and it does not qualify the phrase.

studies.title: They Turned Away Weeping
studies.meaning: The exemption reaches a fourth group, and they are described rather than categorised. They came asking to be carried, were told there was nothing to carry them on, and turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears, grieving that they could find nothing to spend. Nothing is said about their belief or their record. The whole case is made by what happened to their faces.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, at the departure for the march north. The commentators report that a number of men came asking for mounts and were turned away because none were available, and that this ayah was revealed about them. The accounts differ over how many they were and give several names, while agreeing on the incident and its cause.

keyTerms.note: The verb for carrying or providing transport. What they asked for was a mount, since a man on foot could not cross that distance, so the request was practical rather than a plea for inclusion.
The verb is used of a vessel brimming over. The identical phrase appears at 5:83, where it describes people weeping on hearing the revelation, and nowhere else in the Quran.
The noun names sorrow rather than shame or anger. It states the cause of the tears explicitly, and the cause given is not being able to give, which is an unusual thing to grieve over.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A mount was the difference between joining and not joining. The route north ran for weeks across ground where a man on foot carrying his own water would simply not arrive. Camels were expensive and already spoken for. These men were not being refused permission; they were told the equipment did not exist, which nobody could remedy.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing eyes overflowing with tears occurs twice in the Quran. The other place is 5:83, where it describes people weeping on recognising the truth of what they hear. The same image serves for recognition in one passage and for grief at being unable to give in this one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records an intention that produced nothing and treats it as complete. These men gave no money, made no journey, and appear in the surah only as a group walking away in tears. That the Quran preserves them at all is the point: it makes the interior a real thing with standing, rather than a factor weighed alongside outcomes.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for overflowing eyes, there on hearing the revelation.
Names the categories excused, which this ayah extends by describing a single case.
Describes those who could find only their own effort to give, and were mocked for it.

studies.applyIt: Remember something you badly wanted to do and could not, and how quickly you filed it away as nothing. This ayah files it differently. Sit with one of those for a minute this week without correcting it into either an excuse or a failure, and notice that a third category is available.

studies.title: Asking While They Are Rich
studies.meaning: The blame is placed precisely, and the deciding factor is capacity. It falls on those who ask you for exemption while being rich. Then the same two clauses used six ayat earlier return: they were content to be with those left at home, and God sealed their hearts, so they do not know. The repetition makes this ayah the summary of the whole passage on exemptions.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, closing the sequence on who was and was not excused. The commentators read it as the counterpart of 9:91, one naming those on whom there is no blame and this one naming those on whom there is. Between them stand the men who wept, so the passage moves from exemption through a hard case to its opposite.

keyTerms.gloss: the way, the ground for blame
keyTerms.note: Literally a path. In this idiom it means a way to proceed against somebody, so the ayah says there is a case here, where 9:91 had said there is none.
A circumstantial clause giving the condition under which the request was made rather than describing the people themselves. The word means having enough, from the root for sufficiency.
The same verb as at 9:87, there in the passive with no agent named and here in the active with God as its subject. The pair stands six ayat apart and the commentaries read them together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was visible in specific things: the number of date palms a family held, the animals in its pen, the men it could equip. A rich man asking to be excused was making a claim anyone could check within an afternoon. That is why the surah keeps returning to it, and why such a request needed an oath to sustain it.
studies.didYouKnow: Two ayat six lines apart use the same verb for the sealing of hearts, once in the passive with no agent stated and once with God as the subject. The Quran uses both constructions for this image elsewhere, and the classical commentaries treat the pair here as a single statement rather than two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sorts people by capacity as well as by conduct, which produces the surah's unusual result: identical behaviour is blameless in one case and blameworthy in another. That refuses any rule applicable from outside. It also places the sealing after the contentment, keeping the sequence used throughout, in which a state follows a settled preference rather than preceding it.

crossReferences.why: States the opposite, that there is no ground for blame against those who cannot.
Uses the same clauses about contentment and sealed hearts six ayat earlier.
Describes the same request being made by the people of means.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you decline that you could actually afford: money, hours, attention. Not what you cannot manage, which this surah has already excused. The one thing you could do and do not. Name it once, without promising anything, and notice how fast your mind supplies a reason it belongs in the other category.

studies.title: Knower Of The Hidden And The Seen
studies.meaning: The excuses arrive on the return and are refused in advance. Do not make excuses, we will not credit you, God has already informed us about you. Then the sentence widens twice over. God and His Messenger will see what you do; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you. The verb for informing frames both ends.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, on the return from the march north. The commentators note that the passage anticipates a scene rather than reporting one, and that the surah has already described these explanations being prepared. The closing name of God belongs to a group of titles pairing the hidden with the visible, used at moments where concealment is the subject.

keyTerms.note: The verb for conveying news of consequence, used twice in this ayah with God as the subject both times. The sentence is framed by a report already delivered and another still to come.
A paired title covering what is hidden and what is witnessed. Naming both halves removes the distinction the excuse-makers were relying on, which is that some things stay in the first category.
The verb of belief with the preposition meaning to credit a speaker. It refuses the account without disputing any particular sentence in it, which is a different act from calling something false.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A returning expedition brought its own account back, and the men who had stayed heard it before making their own. There was a window, sometimes a day or two, in which explanations were composed and rehearsed. Everyone in a settlement that size knew the window existed, and this passage is placed inside it, arriving before the sentences did.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for informing occurs twice in this ayah, once of a report already given and once of one still to come, with God as the subject both times. The paired name that closes it, covering the unseen and the witnessed together, appears again eleven ayat later at 9:105.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names God by a title covering both halves of what exists, hidden and witnessed, at exactly the moment somebody is relying on the boundary between them. That is how the Quran usually deploys the divine names: not as a list of attributes but as an answer placed where it does work. The name arrives as the refutation rather than as decoration.

crossReferences.why: Ends with the same paired name of God, in a passage about work being seen.
Names God with the same pairing at the head of a long sequence of names.
Uses the same refusal of excuses earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice the assumption underneath any excuse: that some part of the situation stays out of view. Take one explanation you are planning to give and ask what it depends on nobody knowing. You do not have to abandon it. Just see the hidden half clearly, since that is exactly what the name in this ayah addresses.

studies.title: So Turn Away From Them
studies.meaning: The prediction is exact, including its purpose. They will swear to you by God when you come back to them, so that you will turn away from them. The reply grants the request in the same words: so turn away from them. What they wanted was to be left alone, and they are left alone. The rest of the sentence explains why granting it is not a concession.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, on the return from the march north. The commentators read the two clauses as a request granted, since the phrase asked for and the phrase given are identical in Arabic. The surah has been describing oaths sworn to the community throughout this section, and here it names what those oaths were actually for.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to turn one's side toward something and away from it. Their purpose is stated in the same words the reply then uses, so the request and its answer are verbally identical.
A future with an emphatic prefix. The surah uses this verb repeatedly of the same group, and here it announces the oath before it is sworn, which removes its usefulness in advance.
From a verb meaning to take shelter. A word for a place of refuge is used for where they end up, which is a bleak choice given that shelter is what the oaths were seeking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being left alone was a real thing to want. In a settlement where every household's business was public, the ambition of somebody in an awkward position was not vindication but quiet: to stop being asked about, to have the subject drop. An oath was the standard tool for producing that quiet, and it usually worked within a week.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing what they want and the instruction given in reply are the same words in Arabic, request and answer stated identically. The surah grants what is asked and lets the granting carry the judgement, a construction it uses more than once in this section of the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a request by fulfilling it, which is a distinctive move. Nothing is refused and nothing is argued. What the oath was for is simply given, and the sentence then describes what that leaves behind. It suggests some outcomes are indistinguishable from getting exactly what one asked for, which is harder to be warned about than a refusal.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately with a second purpose the same oaths were serving.
Describes oaths taken as a shield by people whose deeds are evil.
Describes people swearing on a falsehood knowingly, using oaths as cover.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you actually want from a conversation you are dreading. Often it is not to be understood but to have the matter dropped. That is a legitimate thing to want and worth naming, because a subject that drops is not the same as a subject that is finished, and only one of them stays finished.

studies.title: Least Likely To Know The Limits
studies.meaning: The oaths have a second purpose: that you be pleased with them. The reply separates two things people ordinarily run together. Even if you are pleased with them, God is not pleased with a people who go past the bounds. The passage then turns to the desert tribes, and the reason given for their condition is distance, since they are the likeliest not to know the limits of what was revealed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators are careful with the second of these ayat, noting that it describes a tendency produced by distance from the community and its teaching rather than a verdict on a people, and that the surah names believing members of the same tribes three ayat later. The two statements are read together across the classical commentaries.

keyTerms.gloss: that you be pleased with them
keyTerms.note: The same root the surah uses for God's acceptance. Here it names a community's approval, and the reply separates the two, saying one does not produce the other in either direction.
A comparative meaning more fitted to something. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it makes the statement a matter of probability rather than of category, which the commentators emphasise.

The word for boundaries of land, extended to the limits set in revelation. What is named as lacking is knowledge of where the edges are, which is precisely what distance from a teaching community produces.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Learning happened by presence. A person in Medina heard revelation recited daily, watched how questions were answered, and absorbed the shape of things by living close to it. Someone three days out with a herd got fragments carried by travellers, months apart and out of order. The difference named here is one of exposure rather than of capacity.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for desert Arabs occurs ten times in the Quran and six of those are in this surah, within a run of about a dozen ayat. Two of the six describe people among them who believe, so the surah making the strongest statement about the group also states the exception a few lines later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to let human approval stand in for divine acceptance, in either direction. A community can be satisfied with someone God is not, which limits what any group's welcome can be taken to mean. The following ayah then explains a moral condition by access to teaching rather than by nature, which turns a description into something capable of changing.

crossReferences.why: Names those among the same tribes who believe, three ayat after this description.
Records desert Arabs claiming faith and being told to say they have submitted.
Uses the same pair of words for God being pleased and people being pleased.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you are treating being approved of as being right. The two come apart more often than it feels. Pick a decision your circle endorses and ask whether you would still hold it in a room of strangers. The exercise is not about defying anyone; it is about seeing which of the two you were tracking.

studies.title: Counting A Gift As A Fine
studies.meaning: Two attitudes are named in one sentence and they belong together. Some treat what they spend as a penalty, and they watch for the turns of fortune to come round against you. Money given to an arrangement one is waiting to see fail is naturally felt as a loss. The reply then turns the same word back on them: upon them is the turn of misfortune.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, describing contributions collected from the tribes around Medina. The commentators read the two clauses as connected, the accounting following from the loyalty rather than the other way about. The surah has been describing contributions throughout this section, and the ayah immediately after gives the opposite case among the same people.

keyTerms.gloss: a fine, a penalty, a loss
keyTerms.note: The word for a debt or a compensation paid out. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it names exactly how a payment feels when the person paying expects nothing back from the arrangement.
A plural from the verb to circle, naming reversals that come round again. The word occurs only once in the Quran and pictures fortune as rotating rather than as rising or falling.
The reply uses the singular of the same word. What they were waiting for is named as arriving at them, so the sentence answers using the very image its speakers had supplied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fortune really did rotate. A tribe strong for a decade could be broken by a drought, a lost battle, or the collapse of a trade route, and everyone had watched it happen to somebody. Betting on a reversal was ordinary political sense rather than malice. Tribes routinely kept relations with two sides precisely because the wheel was known to turn.
studies.didYouKnow: Both distinctive words in this ayah occur only once in the Quran, the term for a fine and the plural for turns of fortune. The singular of the second appears once more at 48:6, so the vocabulary of this sentence belongs almost entirely to two Medinan passages about the same expectation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage connects an accounting to an allegiance. Money given to something a person hopes will fail cannot be felt as anything but a loss, and naming that explains a great deal about reluctant giving without accusing anybody of meanness. The reply then adopts the image of a turning wheel, accepting the premise that fortune rotates and disputing only its direction.

crossReferences.why: Gives the opposite case among the same people, spending taken as nearness.
Uses the same phrase for the turn of misfortune, of those who think ill of God.
Describes contributions given grudgingly, earlier in this same surah.

studies.applyIt: Look at a payment in your life that feels like a fine: a subscription, a levy, a contribution to something you are not sure about. Ask what you are quietly hoping about the thing you are paying into. The feeling usually follows the hope rather than the amount, and the hope is the part you can examine.

studies.title: Taken As Steps Of Nearness
studies.meaning: The opposite case is given among the same people, and the whole difference lies in what a payment is taken to be. Some believe in God and the last day and treat what they spend as means of nearness, and as occasions for the Messenger's prayers. A short interjection then confirms it: they are indeed a nearness for them. The same act is a fine in one ayah and an approach in the next.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the ayah describing contributions treated as a penalty. The commentators note the deliberate pairing and read the two together as showing that the group described earlier was never being characterised as a whole. The word for nearness appears here in a form used nowhere else in the Quran.

keyTerms.note: A plural from the root for closeness, occurring only once in the Quran. Naming a payment as a plurality of approaches makes each act a separate movement toward something rather than one transaction.
The prayers spoken over a contribution when it was brought in. Listing them alongside nearness makes the human response part of what the giver is understood to be seeking.
An interjection confirming what the givers believed. The Quran rarely stops to endorse an intention this directly, and commentators note the emphasis particles standing at the head of the clause.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Contributions from outlying tribes arrived as animals and produce carried in over several days. The man who brought them stood there while they were counted and while a prayer was said over them, and then rode home. That short scene was the whole of his contact with the centre of the community, which is why the prayers mattered as much as the goods.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural word for means of nearness occurs only once in the whole Quran, in this ayah. The singular of the same word closes the sentence a few words later, so the ayah names the giver's intention in a rare plural and then confirms it in the ordinary singular form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the meaning of an act depend on what the actor takes it to be, and then endorses their reading. That is a strong position: the payment is not merely accepted, the giver's understanding of it is confirmed as correct. Coming directly after the opposite case, it shows the same outward act carrying two entirely different contents.

crossReferences.why: Gives the opposite case among the same people, spending treated as a fine.
Describes the Messenger praying over what is collected, four ayat later.
Compares giving that seeks God's acceptance to a garden set on high ground.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you pay for regularly and decide, once, what it is for. Not a new payment. The same one, given a purpose you would say out loud. The whole difference between this ayah and the one before it is what the giver understands themselves to be doing, and that is available to you this afternoon.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: Pleased With Them, And They With Him
studies.meaning: Three groups are named in one sentence: the first to go ahead among those who emigrated, those who gave them shelter, and those who followed them in doing well. Then the clause the ayah is known for, running in both directions. God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. The third group is defined by manner rather than date, which keeps the sentence from closing on one generation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators note that the third group is described by how it follows rather than by when, so the sentence reaches past the people it begins with. The ayah stands among passages about those who held back, and the contrast is deliberate: the surah names the first to move immediately after describing those who did not.

keyTerms.note: The first word names those who outstrip others in a race. It appears again at 56:10 and nowhere else in the Quran, both times of people ahead of the rest rather than merely early.
The condition attached to the third group. It specifies a manner rather than a date, which is why commentators read that group as remaining open rather than closing with a generation.
The clause continues by reversing itself, and they with Him, in the identical verb. It appears four times in the Quran, three of them in the closing ayat of their surahs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Going first cost the most. The earliest emigrants left when the outcome was entirely unknown, and the households in Medina who took them in did so before there was anything at all to gain. Both groups decided without the information everyone who followed later had. That is what the word for going ahead marks: a position in a sequence, not a rank.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God being pleased with them and they with Him appears four times in the Quran, and the other three all fall in the closing ayat of their surahs. This is the only place it occurs in the middle of one, set among passages about people who stayed behind.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a relation running in both directions, using the same verb for God and for the human being. That is rare and it is the point of the sentence. It also defines the third group by a manner rather than a date, so the description is not a monument to one generation but an entry that stays open on stated terms.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same two-way clause, at the very end of that surah.
Describes those who gave shelter and preferred others over themselves despite need.
Uses the same word for those who go ahead, in a very different setting.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the sentence names a third group defined by how they follow rather than when. That is the one still open. Ask what following well would mean this week in one specific thing you inherited from somebody: a practice, a standard, a way of treating people. Then do that thing carefully, once.

studies.title: You Do Not Know Them
studies.meaning: Two populations are named, those around you among the desert tribes and the people of the city itself, and one description covers both. They have become practised at doubleness, worn smooth by it. Then the sentence that gives the passage its weight: you do not know them, We know them. The community's leadership is told plainly that it cannot identify these people, and nothing further is supplied.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators note that the ayah addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly and states a limit on what he knew, which they read as striking given how much of this surah concerns exposure. The passage names nobody, and the tradition preserves no list, which the commentaries treat as deliberate rather than as a gap.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to grow smooth and bare, used of a wall or a plant stripped of its covering. Applied to conduct it means being so accustomed to something that nothing catches on it any more.
A plain statement of a limit, addressed to the one person best placed to know. Commentators note that the surah spends many ayat on exposure and then says this, which is a deliberate arrangement.
A dual, so exactly two occasions are meant. The commentators offer several accounts of what the two are and do not settle among them, which leaves this one of the passage's open questions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A town of a few thousand people knew itself. Everyone's cousins, debts, marriages and quarrels were common property, and reputation was maintained continuously by talk. To be told that some people in such a place could not be identified was to be told something surprising about how well a small community actually sees itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here occurs only once in the Quran, and its root describes a surface worn smooth and bare, like a wall stripped of its plaster. The image is of something that has lost its texture through repetition, which is a physical way of naming a habit that no longer registers to the person who has it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage states a limit on human knowledge at exactly the point where the surah has been most concerned with exposure. Having spent many ayat describing what came to light, it says plainly that some things did not. That combination protects the reader in both directions: it takes concealment seriously and it removes any licence to identify the concealed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the fear that a surah would expose what is in the heart.
Refers to the same group in Medina, with a different kind of warning attached.
Says they would be known by their tone of speech, a different claim about recognition.

studies.applyIt: The one person best placed to see through people is told that he cannot. Take that as permission to stop working out who is genuine in a situation that has been occupying you. You will not settle it, and the surah says so. Spend the attention on what you are doing instead, which is the half you can see.

studies.title: Others Who Admitted It
studies.meaning: A different group appears without warning: others who confessed their wrongs, having mixed a good deed with another that was bad. No excuse is offered and none is asked for. What follows is a particle of hope, that perhaps God will turn toward them. Then an instruction: take from their wealth a charity that cleanses and grows them, and pray for them, because your prayer is a settling for them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators connect these ayat to men who stayed behind, admitted it without offering an explanation, and were left unresolved until this passage came. The reports name several of them and differ in the details. The two ayat move from confession to what was then done, a sequence the surah rarely gives in full.

keyTerms.note: The verb for stirring two things into one another so that they can no longer be separated. It describes a record that is genuinely mixed rather than one mostly good or mostly bad.
Two verbs, one for washing something clean and one from a root meaning increase. Charity is described as doing both at once, removing and adding, which is why both words are needed.
A noun from the root that also gives the calm sent down at 9:26 and 9:40. There it descends in danger; here it names what a human being's prayer provides for somebody else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Confession without an excuse was socially unusual. The expected move for a man in trouble was to produce a reason, find an intermediary, and let the matter be smoothed over. Admitting the thing plainly left him with no protection and nothing to negotiate with, which is why the accounts describe these men as waiting, unresolved, for some time.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing what the Messenger's prayer provides comes from the same root as the calm sent down twice earlier in this surah, at 9:26 and 9:40. In those places it descends during danger; here the same root names what one person's prayer gives to another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches a practical act to a confession. Something is admitted, hope is expressed but not guaranteed, and a concrete step follows that involves money and another person's prayer. Repentance here is not left as an interior event; it is given a body. And what the prayer produces is named as stillness rather than pardon, which keeps the pardon with God.

crossReferences.why: States that God Himself takes the charity, immediately after this instruction.
Describes another case in this surah of confession followed eventually by relief.
Names God as loving those who turn back and those who keep themselves clean.

studies.applyIt: Try saying one thing plainly without the sentence that usually follows it. Not I did this because, just I did this. Most people have never said a single one that way. This passage attaches everything else to that first plain admission, and the admission is the part that takes any courage.

studies.title: He Takes The Charity Himself
studies.meaning: The question is rhetorical and slightly reproachful: do they not know. Two things are then stated as though they were obvious, and the second is the striking one. God accepts repentance, and God takes the charitable gifts, with a verb of receiving into the hand. The commentators note that the giving is described as passing to God rather than to the recipient, and that the ayah joins turning back and giving into one movement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage about people who admitted their failure to join a difficult expedition and offered their wealth as amends. The ayah before instructs that a portion be taken from their property and that they be prayed for. This one answers the anxiety underneath: whether an offering made after a fault is received at all.

keyTerms.note: A verb for accepting something offered, used of a gift that is not refused. It implies a transaction that could have gone the other way, so acceptance is described as a decision rather than an automatic result.
The plain verb for taking in the hand. Using it of charitable gifts is as startling in Arabic as in English, since what is physically handed to a person is described as taken by God.
An intensive form of the same verb used of a human being turning back. God and the person are described with one root, so the turning is mutual, and His is the more frequent of the two.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Charity in Medina was physical and visible. Dates, grain and animals were brought and handed over in public, counted and distributed, and everyone knew who had given what. There was no anonymity in the transaction. Telling givers that the recipient of their sack of dates was God rather than the man holding out his hands reframed an exchange the whole town could watch.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name closing this ayah comes from the same verb used for a person repenting, and the Quran uses that verb of God more often than of human beings. Arabic makes the reciprocity audible: the servant turns and the Lord turns, and the same three letters carry both movements in the same sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Giving is described as received rather than merely observed, which changes its direction. The gift does not go down to someone in need with God watching; it goes to God, who then distributes it. That protects the dignity of the recipient and removes the giver's position of advantage in a single clause. Joining it to repentance makes a further point: material amends and inward turning are parts of one act.

crossReferences.why: Discusses giving openly and secretly, and what each does to a person's wrongs.
Precedes this ayah, instructing that a portion be taken from their wealth to purify them.
Repeats that He accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds.

studies.applyIt: Give something small this week to someone who will never know it came from you. A payment covered, a bill settled, something left where it is needed. The ayah says the transaction is not really between you and them, and giving anonymously is the simplest way to find out whether you believe that.

studies.title: Say: Work
studies.meaning: The instruction is one word: work. Then three sets of eyes are named in order, God, His Messenger, and the believers, running from the widest to the nearest. Then the sentence moves past all of them: you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you. What began as an instruction ends as a report you will be given about yourself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the passage on those whose case had been left open. The commentators read the instruction as addressed to everyone rather than to any particular group, and note that it comes immediately after several ayat in which no verdict was reached. The closing name of God appeared eleven ayat earlier at 9:94, in a passage about excuses.

keyTerms.note: The plain imperative of the verb for doing and working. Nothing is specified and no object is given, and the sentence moves straight to who will see it, which is where the weight lies.
A future with an emphatic prefix, so the seeing is announced rather than warned about. Three subjects follow the verb in sequence, and the human ones are named after God rather than instead of Him.
A passive future. The return is not something anyone performs; it happens, which is why the sentence shifts from imperative to prediction halfway through without any transition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Work in that settlement was visible by default. Fields, wells, markets and building sites were all open, and a man's labour was watched by neighbours whose own livelihood depended on the same season. Nobody worked in private. What this ayah adds is not another observer of the same kind but one who sees the part the neighbours cannot.
studies.didYouKnow: The paired name of God closing this ayah, covering the unseen and the witnessed together, appears earlier in this surah at 9:94, and both times it ends a sentence about being informed of what one did. The two passages use nearly identical wording eleven ayat apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names three observers and then relocates the final account with a fourth. That arrangement takes the community's judgement seriously without letting it be decisive. It also turns the outcome into information rather than a sentence: what is promised is being told what you did, which assumes a person does not fully know their own record while making it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same closing name and the same verb of informing, in a passage about excuses.
States that an atom's weight of good will be seen by the one who did it.
Describes a record produced that leaves nothing out, whether small or large.

studies.applyIt: The instruction is one word with no object attached: work. Pick something today that you have been waiting to feel ready for, and do a piece of it badly. The ayah does not specify what, and it does not mention outcomes. It only names who is watching, which is a different kind of pressure and a lighter one.

studies.title: Held In Suspense
studies.meaning: A third group is named after those who were pardoned and those who confessed. These are held back, deferred to God's command: either He punishes them or He turns toward them. The sentence gives no indication which, and it does not close. What is described is a state of not knowing, and the ayah leaves the reader inside it rather than resolving it on anyone's behalf.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators connect this ayah to specific men whose case remained undecided for a period after the return from the march north, and they report that the resolution came later in the same surah. Read in place, the ayah stands between a passage on confession and one about a building, with nothing settled in it.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from a verb meaning to delay or put off. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it names people whose situation has been left open rather than decided in either direction.

The first half of a construction giving two possibilities with nothing to choose between them. Arabic uses it where both outcomes remain genuinely available, so the grammar keeps the case from closing.
The verb for repentance with God as its subject. It stands second in the pair and is what the sentence ends on, though the construction gives it no more weight than the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting on a judgement was an ordinary and dreadful condition. Disputes went to arbitration and sometimes sat for weeks while an arbitrator travelled or a witness was found, and the parties lived beside each other meanwhile. Everyone in that town had waited on somebody else's decision, unable to plan, going about their business as normal.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing these men as held in suspense occurs only once in the Quran. The surah gives them a single short ayah and then moves to an entirely different subject, leaving their case unresolved on the page for several pages before a resolution arrives much later at 9:118.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names an unresolved state and declines to resolve it, which is unusual in a text that so often supplies verdicts. That leaves the reader holding uncertainty on behalf of people who were holding it themselves. It also implies that not knowing is a real condition a believer can be in, rather than a failure of faith to be talked away.

crossReferences.why: Gives the resolution for men left in this condition, later in the same surah.
Describes the group immediately before these, who confessed and were given hope.
Uses the same verb for deferring, in an entirely different context.

studies.applyIt: Notice something in your life that is genuinely undecided and that you keep trying to settle in your head anyway. Say once, out loud, that you do not know how it will go. This ayah gives a whole category to people in that position, and it does not treat the not knowing as a fault.

studies.title: A Building Meant To Divide
studies.meaning: A building is described by four purposes and none of them is worship: harm, rejection, division among the believers, and a station kept ready for someone who had made war on God and His Messenger before. Then the oath is quoted: we intended only what is good. The reply does not analyse it. God bears witness that they are lying, and the sentence stops there.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, on the return from the march north. The commentators report the incident consistently: a second place of prayer was built near an existing one, its founders asked for it to be endorsed, and this passage came instead. They differ over some details and agree on the purpose the passage names, which is division.

keyTerms.note: A noun of purpose meaning the infliction of injury. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 2:231 of keeping a marriage in order to hurt, and both times names something legitimate used as a weapon.

keyTerms.gloss: and to divide, to split apart
keyTerms.note: From the verb to separate. Naming division as a purpose rather than an effect is the passage's sharpest move, since it treats a rift as something that can be deliberately manufactured.

keyTerms.gloss: and as a lookout, an outpost
keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to lie in wait or watch for. It occurs only once in the Quran and names a place kept ready for somebody, which is a military rather than a devotional use of a building.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A place of prayer was also a meeting hall. It was where news was heard, disputes were raised, travellers were housed and decisions announced. Building a second one a short distance away did not divide worship so much as create an alternative centre of information and gathering, which is what made it a political act in a town that size.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for harm used here occurs twice in the Quran, and the other place, at 2:231, describes holding on to a marriage in order to injure the other person. In both cases the Quran uses this word for something legitimate being maintained precisely so that it can do damage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage judges a religious institution by its purpose rather than by its form. What was built was in every visible respect a place of prayer, and the sentence looks straight past that. It also treats division inside a community as an aim somebody can actually hold, which is a specific and unsentimental claim about how communities come apart.

crossReferences.why: Contrasts it with a place founded on awareness of God from the very first day.
Uses the same word for harm, of maintaining a bond in order to injure.
Instructs holding together and not becoming divided, the state this building targeted.

studies.applyIt: Ask what a group you belong to is actually for, as opposed to what it says it is for. Not to expose anyone. Just to notice the difference where it exists, in a committee, a chat, a standing arrangement. This ayah's method is to state four purposes and let the stated one arrive last.

studies.title: Founded From The First Day
studies.meaning: Two buildings are set against each other by their foundations. Do not stand in that one, ever. A place founded on awareness of God from the first day has more right to your standing in it. Then a clause about people rather than structures: in it are men who love to purify themselves. The building is identified by who is inside it, and the sentence closes on divine love.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately following the description of the building put up to divide. The commentators identify the one founded from the first day with an earlier place of prayer just outside Medina, and preserve accounts of what its people were known for. The contrast is stated in the same terms as the previous ayah, foundation against foundation.

keyTerms.note: The verb for laying a foundation. It appears in this ayah and again in the next one and nowhere else in the Quran, so the whole vocabulary of founding belongs to two consecutive sentences.
The phrase dates the intention to the beginning rather than describing a later state. What is compared is not how two places are used now but what each was for when the ground was broken.
An intensive form describing people who make themselves clean, with the sense of taking pains over it. It occurs only once in the Quran, and the sentence says God loves them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was the word for taking part. A place of prayer was not sat in; people stood in rows, and to stand in one was to be counted among those who used it. The instruction here is therefore about association as much as about worship, and anyone in Medina would have heard it as a statement about which gathering a person belonged to.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for laying a foundation appears in this ayah and in the one immediately following, three times across two sentences, and nowhere else in the Quran. An entire strand of vocabulary belongs to this single passage about two buildings and what each was founded upon.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the character of a place in its origin and in its people, not in its architecture. A building founded on one intention from the first day is described as having a better claim on someone's presence, which makes belonging a question of what a thing was for. And the closing clause attaches divine love to an ordinary habit rather than to a grand act.

crossReferences.why: Describes the building this one is contrasted with, and the purposes behind it.
Continues the comparison as an image of two foundations, one solid and one crumbling.
Describes houses God permitted to be raised and His name remembered in them.

studies.applyIt: Think about where you regularly show up and what it was founded for. A workplace, a group, a routine. Foundations are hard to see once a thing is running, so ask somebody who was there at the start. This ayah treats the answer as deciding something about whether to keep standing there.

studies.title: The Lip Of A Crumbling Bank
studies.meaning: The comparison becomes an image and the image does the arguing. Is the one who founded his building on awareness of God and His acceptance better, or the one who founded his on the lip of an undercut bank, so that it collapsed with him. The second half of the sentence enacts what it describes: the building falls inside the clause, taking its builder down with it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing from the two buildings of the previous ayat. The commentators note that the image is drawn from an ordinary hazard of the region, and read it as generalising the specific case, since neither builder is named here. The passage moves from a particular incident to a question anyone can be asked about their own foundation.

keyTerms.gloss: the lip of an undercut bank
keyTerms.note: The first word means an edge or brink, the second a bank hollowed out underneath by water. The phrase occurs only once in the Quran and names a specific and familiar hazard of that landscape.
An adjective for something on the point of collapse. Its form is unusual and the commentators discuss its derivation, agreeing that it names the moment before a fall rather than the fall itself.

The verb comes from the same root as the adjective two words earlier, so the collapse is announced by the word that described the danger. The phrase adds with him, putting the builder inside the fall.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Watercourses in that landscape cut under their banks in the flood season and left ground that looked solid and was not. Anyone who had built or grazed near a dry riverbed knew the sight: a level surface with nothing beneath it, and a whole edge gone after one night of rain. The image would have registered as a real thing, not a figure of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the collapse comes from the same root as the adjective describing the bank two words earlier, so the sentence uses one root twice in immediate succession. The word for the undercut bank occurs only once in the Quran, and its rarity is why the commentators describe the terrain at some length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the difference between two lives in what lies underneath rather than in what is visible. Both men built, and the sentence does not compare the structures at all. That makes the question unanswerable from outside and answerable from inside, since only the builder knows what he laid the first course on. The image also makes the collapse a matter of time.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the two buildings this image generalises, one founded on awareness of God.
Compares a good word to a tree with firm roots and branches in the sky.
Compares charity spoiled by display to soil on a rock washed bare by rain.

studies.applyIt: Ask what one of your commitments was founded on, at the moment you took it up. Not what keeps it going now, which is usually habit. The original reason. If you cannot recall it, that is worth knowing, and if you can, it is worth checking whether the ground under it is still where you left it.

studies.title: A Doubt That Does Not Leave
studies.meaning: The consequence is interior and it is stated as continuing. The building they built will not cease to be a misgiving in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut apart. What was constructed outside has become something carried inside, and the only end the sentence names is a violent one. Nothing at all is said about what happened to the building. The passage follows the doubt instead.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, closing the passage about the two buildings. The commentators read the ayah as describing what the founders were left with rather than what became of the site, and they discuss the final clause at length, differing over whether the cutting names death or something else. The surah turns to an entirely different subject immediately afterwards.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the root for uncertainty and suspicion. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it names a persistent unease rather than an intellectual question, which is why the sentence offers it no answer.
A construction naming something ongoing with no end supplied. The ayah uses it to make the doubt a condition rather than an episode, continuing for as long as the exception is not met.
An intensive verb meaning to be cut into pieces. The commentators differ over whether the clause names death or a breaking of another kind, and they record the readings without settling between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A building outlives the argument that produced it. In a settlement where structures were mud brick and palm trunk, a wall stood for a generation and was walked past daily by everyone who had been on either side of the dispute. The founders of this one would have seen it, or its site, every day for the rest of their lives.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the doubt that will not go away occurs only once in the Quran, in this ayah, though its root is used earlier in the surah at 9:45 for people wavering back and forth. The rare noun names the settled form of what that earlier passage described as motion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes an act producing a lasting internal condition, the same sequence the surah used at 9:77. Something done outward becomes something carried inward, and it is not undone by the outward thing being dealt with. That is a claim about how actions work on the person who performs them, and it puts the real consequence where nobody else can see it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root for doubt, describing people wavering about inside it.
Describes the same sequence, an act followed by a lasting condition of the heart.
Supplies the image of the two foundations that this ayah closes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you built or arranged for a reason you would not now state out loud. It may still be standing and still working. Notice whether it costs you anything to look at. This ayah is not about the thing itself; it is about what you carry every time you walk past it.

studies.title: A Purchase Already Agreed
studies.meaning: The relationship is described as a completed sale, with a buyer, a price and goods. What is bought is lives and property, and the payment is the Garden, stated as already settled rather than promised on condition. The terms are then said to stand in three scriptures, and a question is asked that has no available answer. The passage ends with an instruction to rejoice at the bargain, which the commentators read as its whole point.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah addressing a community that had been asked to set out on a hard expedition and had divided over it. The commentators connect the language of a completed sale with the pledges given by early supporters in Medina before the migration, and note that the ayah addresses people who had already committed themselves rather than those being recruited.

keyTerms.note: A past-tense verb of purchase. The transaction is described as concluded rather than offered, which is why the closing instruction is to be glad about a sale already made rather than to consider one.
The word for a commercial exchange, and the root behind the pledge of allegiance, which was sealed by clasping hands the way traders did. Both senses are present in the sentence at once.
A phrase used across the Quran for final success. Its placement closes an ayah of commercial vocabulary with a word for winning through, which returns the exchange to the language of rescue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca and Medina lived by trade, and a sale was a public ritual: terms stated aloud, hands struck together, witnesses present. A concluded sale could not be reopened, and a man who tried was disgraced. Describing commitment to God in that language spoke to people who knew exactly how binding a struck bargain was, and how little sympathy a seller with regrets received.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names three scriptures together, the Torah, the Gospel and the Quran, and says the promise stands in all of them. It is one of the few places where the three are listed inside a single clause, and the sequence runs in chronological order, which presents the promise as long standing rather than new.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The transaction is described with God as the buyer, which is the strange part: the one who owns everything is portrayed as purchasing what is already His. Classical commentators read that as a statement about generosity rather than about exchange. And because the sale is announced as concluded, the passage is not recruiting anybody; it tells people what they are already inside, and asks them to be glad of it.

crossReferences.why: Offers the same image as a trade that saves from a painful punishment.
Uses the same commercial language of selling this life for the next.
Describes the pledge given by hand as a pledge given to God Himself.

studies.applyIt: Think of a commitment you made once and have been quietly renegotiating with yourself ever since. Do not reopen it today. Just notice that you have been treating a closed matter as an open one, and that most of the tiredness around it comes from holding the question open rather than from the commitment itself.

studies.title: Nine Words And No Verb
studies.meaning: Nine descriptions are listed with no verb between them, each one a participle: those who turn back, who worship, who praise, who journey, who bow, who prostrate, who call for what is right, who warn against what is wrong, who keep God's limits. Then the sentence turns to somebody else entirely and says give good news to the believers. The list is a portrait rather than a set of instructions.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the ayah about a purchase already agreed. The commentators read the list as describing the people that ayah named, and they differ over the fourth item, some reading it as travelling and others as fasting. Both readings are recorded in the classical commentaries without one being settled.

keyTerms.note: The list opens with repentance rather than with worship, and the word is the one that gives this surah its name. Placing it first makes returning the entry into everything that follows.
The commentators differ genuinely here. Some read a verb of travelling through the earth, others a settled usage meaning those who fast. The word occurs only once in the Quran in this form.
The list ends where the earlier passage about the desert tribes ended, with the limits. What was named as unknown at 9:97 is here named as kept, closing a distance the surah had opened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descriptions of this kind were how a person was introduced. Arabic praise poetry stacked participles rather than sentences, naming a man by his habits in sequence until a picture assembled itself. An audience hearing nine of them in a row would have recognised the form at once, the way a eulogy or a boast was constructed.
studies.didYouKnow: The list contains nine participles and no main verb until the final clause, which turns to address somebody else. The fourth item is one of the places where the classical commentators record two genuinely different readings, travelling or fasting, and transmit both of them rather than choosing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes rather than commands, and the description begins with turning back rather than with any act of worship. That ordering says the door into the list is open at any point, since repentance is the one item that presupposes a prior failure. Ending with the keeping of limits then closes the portrait on restraint rather than on achievement.

crossReferences.why: Describes the exchange this list portrays the parties to, in the ayah immediately before.
Opens a comparable portrait of believers, built the same way from successive descriptions.
Uses the same rare word alongside other descriptions, in a different list.

studies.applyIt: Read the list slowly and find the one item you would least like to be described by, because it is furthest from true. Not to fix it today. Just to know which one it is. Nine descriptions arrive with no instruction attached, and noticing where you fall short of one is the only use a portrait has.

studies.title: Even If They Were Close Kin
studies.meaning: A limit is stated and the hardest case is named inside it. It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for those who associated others with God, even if they were near of kin, after it has become clear to them where those people stand. The clause about relatives is not an exception. It is placed there to say that the closest relationship changes nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators connect the passage to a question about praying for relatives who had died, and preserve several accounts of the occasion with variations between them. The ayah that follows immediately supplies a precedent from the life of Abraham, which is how the surah answers the emotional weight of the case rather than only its structure.

keyTerms.gloss: it is not for the Prophet
keyTerms.note: A construction meaning something does not belong to a person's role rather than that it is barred to them. Arabic uses it to describe what is out of place for someone, which is gentler than a plain negative.
The word for closeness, used of family. Naming the hardest case explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred is what gives the ayah its weight for anyone reading it in grief.
A reflexive verb meaning to become evident of its own accord. The condition attaches to clarity rather than to suspicion, and the same verb governs the precedent given in the following ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayer for the dead was a family obligation and a public one. Sons prayed for fathers, and a man who did not was making a statement everyone would notice within a day. In a society organised entirely by descent, this passage asked people to withhold something that had never been separable from being somebody's child.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for something becoming clear appears in this ayah and again in the next one, where it governs the moment Abraham stopped asking. The same word therefore marks the condition inside the rule and the condition inside the precedent, tying the two ayat together at their hinge.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage states a limit and then, in the following ayah, supplies a prophet who reached the same limit himself and felt its difficulty. That order matters. A hard position is not left as an abstraction; it is shown having been occupied by somebody described in the next line as tender-hearted, which acknowledges the cost without altering the position.

crossReferences.why: Gives the precedent from Abraham's life, and the reason his own asking stopped.
Records the same episode, Abraham's promise to his father, as an exception to an example.
States that guidance is not in the hands of even the most devoted person.

studies.applyIt: There is a kind of grief that comes from wanting to fix somebody's standing after they are gone. If you carry any of it, notice that this passage puts a prophet in exactly that position in its very next line, and calls him tender-hearted for it. The feeling is nowhere corrected. Only the action is.

studies.title: A Promise He Had Made
studies.meaning: The precedent is given with its reason attached. Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him; when it became clear that his father stood against God, he separated himself. Then a sentence that changes the temperature completely. Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing. The ayah explains the stopping and then defends the man who found it hard.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, supplying a precedent for the limit stated in the previous ayah. The commentators connect the promise mentioned here to the parting recorded elsewhere in the Quran, where Abraham tells his father he will ask forgiveness for him. This ayah reports how that promise ended, which the earlier passages do not.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the verb to promise. The whole explanation rests on it: the asking is presented as keeping a word given earlier rather than as a judgement about how things would turn out.
From the same root as the word that opens this surah, where it names the ending of treaty obligations. One root covers the dissolving of a public pact and this private separation.
A rare word describing someone who cries out from grief or compassion. It occurs only once in this form, and the same pair of adjectives is applied to Abraham again at 11:75.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise made at a parting was among the strongest things a person could give. Travel was slow and often final, and words said at a departure were remembered for decades by both sides. Abraham's undertaking to his father belonged to that kind of moment, which is why the ayah treats keeping it as needing no defence at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for separating himself comes from the same root as the word that opens this entire surah, where it names the ending of treaty obligations. The surah's first word and this private parting between a son and his father are built from the same three letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage explains a hard action by an earlier promise and then, having explained it, praises the man's softness rather than his firmness. That combination is the point. Doing a difficult thing is not taken as evidence of a hard character, and the ayah says so in the same sentence, which protects anyone who has had to do something similar.

crossReferences.why: Records the promise itself, where Abraham tells his father he will ask forgiveness for him.
States the limit that this precedent is given to illustrate, in the ayah before.
Uses the same two adjectives of Abraham, tender-hearted and forbearing.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order of this ayah: it explains the hard act first, then names the softness of the man who did it. If you have had to hold a line with somebody you love, you may have concluded that doing so made you cold. This ayah puts both things in one sentence and does not treat them as contradicting.

studies.title: Clarity Comes First
studies.meaning: A principle is stated in the negative, which is where its force comes from. God would never let a people go astray after having guided them until He makes clear to them what they should guard against. Clarity comes first and accountability follows it, in that order and not the reverse. The sentence closes on knowledge, which is what the whole claim rests upon.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the passage about Abraham and the limit on asking forgiveness. The commentators read the ayah as answering an anxiety produced by that limit: whether people could be held to something they had done before it was stated. The answer given is general rather than tied to the particular case.

keyTerms.note: The verb for causing someone to stray. The sentence denies it of God under a specific condition, so what is ruled out is a verdict passed before the terms were given rather than straying in general.
The same verb used in the two previous ayat for something becoming evident, here in a form meaning to make evident. The passage moves from things becoming clear to God making them so.
From the verb meaning to shield oneself. What is promised as made clear is not everything but specifically the things to keep clear of, which is a narrower and more practical undertaking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rules that arrived after the fact were a real grievance in that world. A tribe could find itself judged by a custom it had never been told, and arbitrators were expected to state the basis of a decision before applying it. The principle this ayah puts in a religious register was already the standard by which a fair judge was recognised.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for something becoming clear runs through three consecutive ayat here, at 9:113, 9:114 and 9:115. In the first two it describes a realisation arriving; in the third it describes God making something plain, so the root moves from what people come to see to what is shown to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes clarity a precondition of accountability, which is a statement about the character of God rather than about procedure. It also implies that guidance can be lost, since the sentence concerns a people who already had it. Both halves matter: the standard is high, and the protection offered is that nobody answers for a line they were never shown.

crossReferences.why: States that no one is punished until a messenger has been sent to them.
Says communities are not destroyed for wrongdoing while their people remain unaware.
Uses the same verb for clarity, in the condition attached to the limit stated there.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether the people around you actually know what you expect of them. Not whether they should know. Whether you have said it. This ayah puts clarity before accountability and describes that as how God deals with people, which makes it an uncomfortable standard for a manager, a parent, or a friend.

studies.title: He Gives Life And Causes Death
studies.meaning: The sentence is short and moves from the largest scale to the most personal in two clauses. To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and He causes death. Then the consequence, addressed directly to the listener: besides God you have no protector and no helper. What began as a statement about ownership ends as a statement about the reader's own situation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, placed between the principle about clarity and the passage on the hour of hardship. The commentators read it as grounding what surrounds it, since a discussion of who may be asked for forgiveness and who is answerable rests on a claim about who holds authority. The formula appears in several places in the Quran with small variations.

keyTerms.note: The noun for possession carrying authority, not merely ownership. Applied to the heavens and the earth together it covers everything that exists, which is why nothing is left over for the clause that follows.

keyTerms.gloss: He gives life and causes death
keyTerms.note: Two verbs in the present tense, describing something ongoing rather than done once. The pairing recurs through the Quran and always names both directions rather than only the giving.
Two words covering different kinds of support, one who takes charge of a matter and one who assists in it. Naming both closes off the whole range rather than a single kind of reliance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection was always somebody's job. A person had a patron, a clan, an ally, and if all three failed, a claim on the sanctuary. Nobody in that world stood alone by choice, and the arrangements were constantly maintained. A sentence saying there is no protector besides God was not abstract; it named every arrangement its listeners actually had.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words for protector and helper appears together repeatedly in the Quran, and within this surah it also closes 9:74, the passage about people who resented having been enriched. The same two words therefore end both a warning and this statement about who holds dominion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds a moral limitation in a claim about ownership. Because everything belongs to God, the question of who may intercede and who is answerable has a single location, which the surah has spent many ayat approaching. Naming life and death together also puts the reader inside the claim, since both verbs describe something that will happen to them.

crossReferences.why: Ends with the same pair of words for protector and helper, in a different setting.
States the same thing about dominion and the absence of any other patron.
Repeats the claim about the dominion of the heavens and the earth.

studies.applyIt: List the three arrangements you rely on most: a job, a person, a savings account. Do not disparage any of them; this ayah does not. Just notice that each is itself dependent on something further back, and follow one of those chains for a minute until it runs out. That is the whole exercise.

studies.title: The Hour Of Hardship
studies.meaning: God turned toward the Prophet, the emigrants and the helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group among them had almost swerved. Then He turned toward them. What is remarkable is the inclusion. The ayah records that people who came, and stayed, nearly did not, and it names that near-failure in the same sentence as the turning.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, referring to the march north. The commentators explain the phrase for the hour of hardship as naming the expedition itself, undertaken in heat, at a great distance, with severe shortages of mounts, water and provisions. The reports describe men sharing a single camel and rationing dates, and the phrase became the standard name for that campaign.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs only once in the Quran and became the name by which that expedition was afterwards known. The second word covers difficulty of every kind, from shortage of supplies to hardship of the road.
The verb names a straying to one side rather than a turning back. Paired with a word meaning almost, it records something that did not happen and that no observer would ever have known about.
The first word names a gentleness that acts to spare somebody difficulty. The pair closes this ayah and appears again at 9:128, so the surah's own ending uses the same two names.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The accounts of that expedition describe conditions that would end most campaigns: men taking turns riding one animal, water rationed by the mouthful, dates counted out a few each per day. Some reports say a single date was passed from man to man. That is what the phrase for the hour of hardship names, and everyone who first heard it had been there.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the hour of hardship occurs only once in the Quran, and the campaign it refers to was afterwards known by that name in the historical sources. The two names of God that close this ayah, for tenderness and for mercy, also close the surah itself at 9:128.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records that the people who succeeded nearly did not, and it does so while confirming that God turned toward them. Nothing is smoothed over. That changes what an accepted action looks like: it can contain a near-failure no observer would have detected, and the acceptance covers the whole of it rather than only the part that held.

crossReferences.why: Continues with the three whose case had been deferred, in the same movement of turning.
Describes another moment when hearts reached the throats and believers were badly shaken.
Closes the surah with the same two names of God used here.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you saw through that you almost abandoned, and that nobody knew you almost abandoned. This ayah puts exactly that on the record beside the outcome. Tell one person about the part where you nearly stopped. It is a small thing to do and it changes how the finishing sits with you.

studies.title: The Earth Closed In On Them
studies.meaning: The three are named only as those who were left behind, and their state is described from the outside inward. The earth narrowed on them despite all its width, then their own selves narrowed on them, and they understood that there was no refuge from God except toward Him. Then He turned toward them so that they might turn. The relenting comes first and the repenting follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, closing the account of the march north.
