The commentators report that three men stayed behind without an excuse, admitted it plainly, and were then set apart from the community for a period of some weeks until this passage came. The reports name them and describe the isolation in detail, agreeing on its length and its ending.

keyTerms.note: A passive form: they were left rather than they stayed. Related forms run through this whole section for a different group, so the word itself does not distinguish between the cases.
The phrase occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah. At 9:25 it describes a battlefield closing in during a rout; here the same effect is produced by other people's silence.

keyTerms.gloss: a refuge, a place to flee
keyTerms.note: The word for shelter appears twice in this surah. At 9:57 men would bolt for one if they could find it; here the only refuge from God is named as God, which closes every direction of escape.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being cut off in a town of that size was total. Nobody spoke to them, no greeting was returned, and their own households were told to keep apart. The reports describe one of the men going to the market where he had traded all his life and being looked straight through. That is what the ayah means by the earth narrowing while remaining wide.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the earth narrowing despite its width occurs only twice in the Quran, both times in this surah. At 9:25 it describes an army breaking apart in a valley, and here it describes three men in a town where nobody would speak to them. One image serves for a rout and for social isolation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the sentence carries its argument. God turned toward them so that they might turn, which puts the divine movement first and makes the human one its consequence. That reverses the usual picture of repentance as something offered up and then accepted. It also means the closing of every other exit was not the punishment but the means.

crossReferences.why: Describes men left in suspense awaiting God's decree, whose case this ayah resolves.
Uses the same closing pair of divine names, fourteen ayat earlier in this surah.
States the general principle that nobody should despair of God's mercy.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the relief here arrives only after every exit had closed, and that the closing was not the point of it. If you are in something with no way out at the moment, this passage does not promise a timeline. It describes three people who had none either, and names what they finally understood.

studies.title: Be With The Truthful
studies.meaning: Two instructions in a very short ayah, and the second is unusual. Not be truthful, but be with the truthful. The commentators note the difference: what is asked for is company, which places character in the plural. Some read the word as those who tell the truth, others as those whose whole state matches what they claim, and the Quran uses it in both senses. Nothing is said about how a person becomes such a one, only about proximity.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the account of three men who stayed behind from a difficult expedition and, unlike others, told the truth about why. The ayat just before describe their isolation and its end. The commentators read this instruction as the conclusion drawn from their case, which makes the truthful in question specific people the audience could name.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth and for what is solid and reliable. The word covers honest speech and a life that matches it, and the same root gives the term used for a formal charitable gift.
A plain preposition of company. Its use makes the instruction relational: the reader is not told to become something but to be near people who already are, and the difference is clearly deliberate.
From a root for shielding oneself. It is paired here with the command about company, so an inward disposition and an outward association are placed side by side as a single instruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in a town the size of Medina was cumulative and unforgettable. Everyone knew who had spoken accurately about a bad harvest and who had shaded it, and a man's word decided whether he could borrow, marry well, or lead. The three men who admitted staying behind took the harder route in a place where their admission would be remembered by everyone for years.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 9 is the only one of the Quran's hundred and fourteen that does not open with the formula naming God as Gracious and Merciful, and the earliest collectors discussed whether it and the surah before it had been one chapter or two. This instruction arrives near the end of it, in one of the three shortest ayat the surah contains.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is presented as something maintained by company rather than by resolve alone. That is a claim about how people actually change: not by deciding to be truthful but by spending time where truthfulness is ordinary. It also makes the instruction available to someone who is not yet what they should be, since being near a quality comes before possessing it. Awareness of God is placed first, and the two are given together.

crossReferences.why: Names the truthful among the company promised to those who obey.
Precedes it, describing the three whose truthfulness this instruction follows from.
Describes men true to what they pledged, and God rewarding the truthful for their truth.

studies.applyIt: Look at where your unstructured time goes and identify one person or group that makes exaggeration feel normal, and one that makes it feel awkward. Spend an extra hour this week with the second. The ayah does not ask you to be better on your own; it points at the room you are standing in.

studies.title: Thirst, Fatigue And Hunger
studies.meaning: The reason is given as an accounting. Nothing that happens on such a journey goes unrecorded: no thirst, no fatigue, no hunger, no step taken that unsettles an opponent, nothing gained from an enemy, without a good deed being written for them. The list is made of discomforts rather than achievements, and each is entered separately. The closing clause says no reward is wasted.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, after the account of the march north. The commentators read the ayah as explaining why staying behind was out of place, and note that the argument given is about what is gained rather than about what is owed. The physical conditions listed match the reports of that expedition closely, particularly the thirst.

keyTerms.note: The word for the thirst of the road rather than ordinary dryness. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it heads a list that moves from the most immediate physical hardship outward.
From a root meaning a hollow or a drawing in of the belly. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 5:3, both times of hunger severe enough to change what a person can do.
A noun of place from the verb to tread. It occurs only once in the Quran and reduces the unit of account to a single step of ground, which is the smallest item in the whole list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Thirst was the governing fact of that march. Wells along the northern route lay far apart and some were low by late summer, and men rode a full day between them carrying what they could. The reports of the expedition dwell on water more than on anything else, which is why it is the first thing this ayah names.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the hardships in this list are named by words that occur only once each in the whole Quran, the thirst and the place trodden. The ayah reduces the unit of account to a single footstep, and the word it uses for that step is found nowhere else in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage counts suffering rather than results. Thirst, tiredness and hunger are entered in the record as good deeds, and so is a single step of ground, which means the ledger is not kept in outcomes at all. That has a consequence for anyone whose effort produced nothing: the entry was made when the effort was made, not when it worked.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same accounting, adding expenditure and the crossing of a valley.
States that nothing done by any worker among them is lost, male or female.
Says an atom's weight of good will be seen by the one who did it.

studies.applyIt: Make a list of what a difficult thing this week actually cost you: the hour lost, the meal missed, the conversation you dreaded. Write the items separately rather than as one lump. This ayah keeps its ledger that way, in units small enough to notice, and the noticing is the part you can do.

studies.title: Small Or Large, It Is Recorded
studies.meaning: The accounting continues and widens. No expenditure, small or large, and no valley crossed, without it being recorded for them, so that God may repay them according to the best of what they did. Two of the three items are entirely ordinary: money spent, ground covered. The final clause changes the arithmetic, since the repayment is set by the best of the work rather than by its average.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing directly from the previous ayah. The commentators read the pair as one argument. The crossing of a valley was the practical unit of a journey in that terrain, since a route was described by the valleys it passed through, so the ayah counts a march in the terms its audience would themselves have used.

keyTerms.note: The pair covers a whole range, in the construction the surah uses elsewhere for light and heavy. Naming the small amount first is deliberate, since that is the one a person would not have counted.
The unit by which a route was described in that country. Counting valleys rather than days or distances measures a journey the way the people making it would have measured it themselves.

keyTerms.gloss: the best of what they did
keyTerms.note: A superlative. The repayment is set by the highest point of the record rather than by its average, which the commentators note as a specific and unusually generous rule of accounting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A journey was told in valleys. Directions were given by naming them in order, and a traveller returning described where he had been by listing which ones he had crossed. The unit was practical: each valley meant a descent, a bed of loose stone and a climb, and crossing one was the day's real work rather than the distance covered.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah measures a journey in valleys crossed, which was how routes were actually described in that landscape. It measures money by naming the smallest and largest amounts together, and then sets the repayment by the best of what was done rather than by the sum, so nothing in it works like an ordinary ledger.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records everything and then repays by the best of it. Those are two different operations, and holding both is the point: nothing is missed, and nothing is averaged. That protects a person from their own worst days without pretending those days did not happen. It also means size does not determine treatment, since small and large are entered alike.

crossReferences.why: Begins the same accounting with thirst, fatigue and hunger on the road.
States that God rewards them according to the best of what they did.
Describes a small expenditure multiplied many times over in the reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Think of the smallest thing you gave away this month, the one too minor to remember. This ayah names small before large. Give something that size again today without deciding whether it is worth anything, and notice that the only reason it felt like nothing was that you were doing the arithmetic yourself.

studies.title: Not All Of Them Should Go
studies.meaning: The instruction turns in the opposite direction from everything before it. The believers should not all march out together. Let a group from each division go, so that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them. After many ayat about failing to move, the surah says that some staying is exactly right, and gives learning as the reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, after the long section on those who stayed behind. The commentators discuss which group the ayah describes as remaining, and record more than one reading: some hold that those who go out are the ones who gain understanding, others that those who stay do. Both readings are transmitted, and the grammar allows either.

keyTerms.note: The same word used at 9:36 of both sides fighting collectively. Here it is what is being ruled out, so the surah uses one term for a total mobilisation and then denies it.
A verb meaning to acquire deep comprehension rather than information. It occurs only once in the Quran in this form, and the whole instruction is built around it as its purpose.
A word for a portion of a larger body. The ayah uses it for what is sent from each division, so what is described is a distribution of tasks rather than a general summons to everyone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Learning had to be carried. There were no copies to send and no schools to attend, so understanding travelled in the memory of a person who had been present and then went home. A tribe three days out depended entirely on whichever of its men had spent time in Medina, which is why the ayah treats the return journey as part of the purpose.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for gaining deep understanding occurs only once in the Quran, in this ayah, and the noun formed from the same root became the ordinary Arabic word for the study of religious law. An entire discipline takes its name from a word the Quran uses a single time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage divides a community's labour and treats learning as one of its tasks rather than as a private matter. It also arrives directly after many ayat criticising people who stayed, which means it draws a distinction the surah has been careful to earn: staying for a purpose and staying to avoid something are not the same act, however similar they look.

crossReferences.why: Instructs everyone to go out, light or heavy, which this ayah then qualifies.
States that those who know among God's servants are the ones who stand in awe.
Records the prayer asking God to increase the one receiving revelation in knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether the thing you are not doing is being skipped or being traded. There is a real difference, and it usually shows in whether anything is happening in its place. Name one thing you have stepped back from and say what you are doing instead. If nothing is, that is worth knowing plainly.

studies.title: Those Who Are Next To You
studies.meaning: The instruction is bounded at its front by a word about proximity: those of the rejecters who are next to you. Commentators read the phrase as naming nearness rather than a category, and they differ over whether it directs a sequence, dealing with what is closest first, or something else. A clause about firmness follows, and then a closing clause placing the whole thing under awareness of God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, near the end of the surah. The commentators place it in the setting of the northern frontier and read the instruction about proximity in practical terms, as concerning the parties actually engaged rather than as an open direction. Several note the closing clause as limiting what precedes it, since it makes the whole instruction conditional on restraint.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to be adjacent or to follow immediately. It occurs only once in the Quran, and commentators differ over whether it names geographical nearness, a sequence of dealing, or both.
A noun for hardness of surface, used of a coat or a wall. It occurs only once in the Quran and describes a quality to be met with rather than an action to be carried out.
The closing clause places the whole instruction under this condition, and commentators note that it is what limits the firmness just named. The same clause closes 9:36 as well.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Frontier conflict in that region was a matter of adjacency. A settlement dealt with the tribes at its edges, because those were the ones that could reach it and be reached, and alliances were built outward one neighbour at a time. The phrase about those next to you would have been heard as a description of how any campaign was actually conducted.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the three distinctive words in this ayah occur only once each in the Quran, the verb for being adjacent and the noun for firmness. The closing clause, that God is with those who guard themselves, appears earlier in this surah at 9:36, where it also follows an instruction about fighting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes on a condition rather than on an encouragement. Firmness is named and then placed under the requirement of guarding oneself, which the commentators read as the limit upon it. That ordering matters for how the sentence works: the last word is not about the opponent at all, but about the state the person acting is required to be in.

crossReferences.why: Ends with the same clause about God being with those who guard themselves.
States the limit directly, that one should not transgress in fighting.
Instructs inclining toward peace whenever the other side inclines toward it.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the sentence ends with a condition on the one acting rather than with anything about an opponent. When you next have to be firm about something, decide in advance what state you intend to be in while doing it. That is the half of this ayah a reader can apply, and it is the half placed last.

studies.title: Which Of You Has This Increased
studies.meaning: A question is quoted rather than answered: whenever a surah is sent down, some of them say, which of you has this increased in faith. The reply does not argue with the sarcasm. It reports two outcomes from one cause. As for those who believe, it increased them in faith, and they take it as good news. Revelation is described as doing different things to different people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, near the end of the surah. The commentators note that this and the following ayat describe a reaction to the arrival of revelation itself rather than to any of its content, and that the surah returns to this scene three times within a few ayat. The question quoted is put in the form of a challenge.

keyTerms.note: The phrase appears three times in the closing part of this surah, at 9:86, 9:124 and 9:127, each time introducing a different reaction to one and the same event.

keyTerms.gloss: so it increased them in faith
keyTerms.note: The verb takes faith as a measurable quantity that can grow. The Quran uses this construction repeatedly, which implies belief is not a single state a person either has or lacks.

keyTerms.gloss: they take it as good news
keyTerms.note: A form meaning to receive something gladly as news. The word describes a reaction rather than a belief, so the passage measures the effect of revelation by what it produces on arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: New revelation arrived as a public event. It was recited, learned and repeated across the settlement within a day, and everyone present had a reaction that others could see. In a place that small, how a person's face changed when a passage was recited was itself a piece of information, which is what these closing ayat are recording.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing a surah being sent down appears three times in the last part of this surah, at 9:86, at 9:124 and at 9:127. Each time it introduces a different response to the same event, so the surah ends by cataloguing the reactions to its own arrival.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says one cause produces two effects, which locates the difference in the receiver rather than in what is received. That has consequences for anyone reading: the text is not the variable. It also treats faith as something that increases, so a person is not fixed at a level, and the same encounter can move them either way.

crossReferences.why: Describes faith increasing when God's signs are recited to the believers.
Gives the other outcome from the same cause, in the very next ayah.
States that the Quran is healing for believers and adds only loss for wrongdoers.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you do with a piece of advice you did not ask for. The same sentence lands differently depending on what is already in the room. Take one thing somebody said to you recently that irritated you, and read it again as though a friend had said it. The words have not changed.

studies.title: Tested Once Or Twice A Year
studies.meaning: The other outcome is given from the same cause. For those with sickness in their hearts, it added to what was already there. Then a question widens the frame: do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year, and still do not turn back or take heed. What is described is not a single refusal but a pattern that survives repeated occasions to break it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators discuss what the yearly testing refers to and record several readings, including hardship, illness, and the recurring demands of the community's situation. They agree that the ayah describes something regular rather than exceptional, which is what gives its point about a pattern outlasting its own interruptions.

keyTerms.note: The Quran uses illness rather than a moral term for this condition, which makes it something that develops and might be treated. The image runs through several surahs and is always located in the heart.
The same noun is used twice within three words, so the increase is described as more of the same rather than as something new arriving. The construction makes the addition cumulative.
The passive of the verb for testing metal by fire, used across this surah for both trial and discord. Here it names a recurring occasion, which the ayah then counts by the year.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The year had its own hard seasons. The gap before a harvest, the summer heat, the demands of a campaign, the arrival of a debt: everyone in that community met a handful of genuinely difficult stretches annually, and everyone knew who they were during one. The ayah is counting those and asking what they produced.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah pairs with the one before it to give two outcomes from a single cause, and the pairing uses almost identical grammar: as for those who believe, and as for those in whose hearts is sickness. The two clauses are built to match, so the difference between them lies in the subject rather than the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures a condition by what repeated occasions fail to change. A pattern that survives one or two annual crises is not an opinion but something settled, and naming it as sickness rather than as wickedness keeps it in the register of what might in principle be treated. The question is left open rather than answered, so the pattern is still running.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other outcome from the same cause, in the ayah immediately before.
Names the same sickness in the heart and says that God increased it.
Uses the same verb for testing, asking whether people expect to be left untried.

studies.applyIt: Count the genuinely hard stretches you had last year, and ask what each one changed. Not whether you got through them; you evidently did. Whether anything is different because of them. This ayah's question is about repetition without effect, and it is worth putting to yourself once a year rather than never.

studies.title: Is Anyone Seeing You
studies.meaning: The scene is small and precisely observed. A surah is sent down, and they look at one another: is anyone seeing you. Then they slip away. The verb for slipping away is picked up immediately and turned around, since God is then said to have turned their hearts away. What they did with their bodies is described as having happened to their hearts, using one root twice in a single sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, the third of three scenes in this closing section describing reactions to a surah arriving. The commentators note the physical detail, the exchanged glance and the checking for observers, and read the passage as describing a gathering in which leaving unnoticed was possible but not easy. The scene is reported rather than judged until its last clause.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to turn oneself away and depart. It occurs only once in the Quran, and the sentence uses its root again two words later with God as the subject.
The same root as the verb just used of their bodies leaving the room. What they did physically is then said of their hearts, so one movement is described at two levels.
A quoted question, given in direct speech. Its concern is entirely with observation rather than with what was being recited, which is precisely what the ayah is recording about them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gatherings for recitation were held in the open, in rows, with everyone's position visible. Leaving early was possible but conspicuous, which is why the question quoted here is about being seen rather than about being stopped. Anyone who has slipped out of a small room while something was being said knows the exchanged glance this ayah records.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for slipping away occurs only once in the Quran, and the very next words use the same root with God as the subject, turning their hearts. A single root does both halves of the sentence, so their departure and its consequence are named with one word used twice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage matches an act to its consequence in form as well as in content, which the surah has done repeatedly. They turned away, and their hearts were turned. It also grounds the outcome in a failure of understanding rather than of will, which keeps the description from being a verdict on their intentions and locates the difficulty in what they could not see.

crossReferences.why: Describes a different reaction to the same event, three ayat earlier.
Uses the same matching construction, they forgot God and He forgot them.
States that God turned their hearts aside when they deviated, in similar terms.

studies.applyIt: Notice the question inside the quotation: is anyone seeing you. It is about the room, not about what was said. Catch yourself once this week checking who is watching before you decide something, then make the decision again with that consideration removed, and see whether it comes out the same.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among You
studies.meaning: Four descriptions in a single line, and the first is about origin: he is from among yourselves, which the commentators read as one of you rather than a stranger sent in. Then his hardship at your hardship, using a word for something weighing heavily. Then eagerness for you. The last two terms are divine names elsewhere in the Quran, applied here to a human being, which is rare and which the commentators remark on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second to last ayah of the surah and, according to several reports, among the final passages of the Quran to be revealed. The surah has been severe throughout, dealing with people who withheld and evaded, and it closes by turning to the character of the man who had been doing the asking. The commentators note the contrast between the surah's tone and its ending.

keyTerms.note: The phrase means something is hard for him to bear. The same word elsewhere describes might and rarity, so the sentence says your difficulty is costly to him, in the vocabulary of value.
A strong word, used elsewhere of greed and of clinging to life. Applied to his concern for people, it describes an appetite rather than a duty, which is what makes the description warm.
A word for gentleness towards someone in difficulty, finer than the general term for mercy. It is used of God in many places, and here it is given to a man, paired with the word for mercy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader in Arabia was expected to be formidable, generous and unmoved. Poetry praised chiefs for endurance and for hospitality, not for anxiety about their followers' distress. Grief expressed on someone else's behalf belonged to the public rituals of mourning. Describing a leader as troubled by what troubles his people named something the surrounding culture did not obviously admire.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words closing this ayah are both used of God elsewhere in the Quran, and this is one of very few places where such a pair is applied to a human being. Classical commentators note the point, treating the shared vocabulary as a statement about the messenger's role rather than about his nature.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is described here through temperament rather than through miracle or authority. What qualifies the messenger, in this sentence, is that other people's suffering costs him something. Naming his origin first makes the same point structurally: the message is not delivered from outside the human situation but from inside it. And placing this at the end of a severe surah suggests the severity was never separable from the concern.

crossReferences.why: Explains the same gentleness as a mercy from God and shows what it prevented.
States his sending as a mercy to all the worlds, in a single line.
Describes him almost destroying himself out of concern that they will not believe.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose difficulty you know about and have filed under sympathy rather than cost. Let it be expensive for an hour: sit with what it would actually be like. The ayah describes a man for whom other people's hardship was heavy, and it names that weight as the qualification, not as a side effect.

studies.title: God Is Enough For Me
studies.meaning: The surah ends on a sentence given to be said. If they turn away, say: God is enough for me, there is no god but He, on Him I have relied, and He is the Lord of the great Throne. The conditional matters. What is supplied is not an argument to win anyone back but a position to hold if nothing works, and the whole reply faces God rather than the people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, the last ayah of the surah. The commentators note that after more than a hundred ayat of proclamation, argument, campaign and exposure, the closing instruction concerns what to say when none of it lands. The phrase itself appears elsewhere in the Quran, and the title of God that ends it appears in two other places.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs twice in the Quran, here in the singular and at 39:38. The surah has already used its plural form at 9:59, in a sentence about being content with a disappointing share.
The verb stands in the past tense, so the reliance is stated as already done rather than as a resolution being formed. Arabic uses this to describe a settled position rather than an intention.

A title appearing three times in the Quran. Ending a surah about treaties, campaigns and internal division with an image of the widest possible authority sets the whole of it against a different scale.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A last word mattered. Arabic speech ended on its strongest line, and a poem or an oration was remembered by how it closed. An audience hearing a long and difficult recitation would have been waiting for the final sentence, and this one hands the speaker something to say rather than something to think, which is the practical form such an ending took.
studies.didYouKnow: The declaration that God is enough occurs twice in this surah, once in the plural at 9:59 as words the surah wishes a discontented group had spoken, and here in the singular as the sentence the surah ends on. The same phrase begins as a wish and finishes as an instruction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah closes by handing over a sentence rather than a conclusion. Everything before it concerned outcomes that depended on other people, and the last ayah supplies a position that does not. It also ends on a title of God naming the widest possible authority, which sets the preceding hundred and twenty-eight ayat against a scale on which they are small.

crossReferences.why: Uses the plural form of the same declaration, as words a discontented group might have said.
Contains the same phrase, spoken in answer to those who rely on other powers.
Records the same declaration made by people facing a gathered force.

studies.applyIt: Learn this sentence and keep it for the moment when an effort you have made does not land. It is short and it is given as a conditional, for exactly that case. Say it once out loud today, before you need it, so that the words are already in your mouth when the moment arrives.
